The Marquis Durazzo, at first in favour of his daughter's entering the Institute, now opposes it, citing various negative judgements about it. Not at all troubled, since they are slanders, she has invited him to apply to the Cardinal Protector. She briefly touches on the opinions against the Institute, bringing out the true situation.

Most Reverend Excellency

1. Not knowing to whom better to turn to confide my anguish than to Your Most Reverend Excellency, to have at once a line of comfort and some relief amid so many troubles, I set everything before you quite frankly.

2. The daughter of the Marquis Durazzo came here to our poor Institute to become a Religious of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate. Everything was arranged in perfect harmony.1

3. After several days the said Marquis wrote to suspend the clothing because he had received bad reports of our poor Institute. First, that it is directed by the Missionaries and not by the Jesuits;2 secondly, that our Protector is a layman and not a Cardinal, whereas by God's mercy we have a holy Cardinal.3

4. That we have debts, that our Rule cannot be approved, and that in time we shall fall under the wicked of these times.4

5. You can imagine how wounded I felt after having toiled so much and suffered for the Lord, my only thought. It was a mortal blow to me, but I was not at all troubled, since it is all slander; I simply replied calmly: apply to our

Protector, Cardinal Vannicelli, and you will hear the truth from him.

6. About the Rule I say nothing, for Your Excellency is better informed than I. As for debts, I can assure you we have none; we live on Providence, which never fails in any of the Houses, of which there are already six.

7. You know Signor Tornatore well enough, and the Missionaries who direct the Houses where they are present; the Houses where there can be no Missionaries are directed by Parish Priests appointed by the Diocesan Bishop himself.5 I have set this out quite frankly and beg you to find a way to lessen — indeed to remove — these slanders; I hope for everything from Your Excellency, in whom I place all my trust.

8. A line from His Eminence would smooth everything; I await it anxiously; believe me, I shall be eternally indebted to you for this favour.6

9. I beg you to present my respects to His Eminence and obtain for me his Fatherly Apostolic Blessing, adding your own, as I remain Your Excellency's

most humble Sr. A. MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

She has received the sad news: the Rule must be withdrawn and burnt, and Fr Tornatore removed from the Institute. Ready to do God's will, she has given instructions accordingly. She asks to be allowed to go to Rome to give the necessary explanations and receive advice.

Most Reverend Excellency,

1. Yesterday, a few hours after sending a letter to Your Excellency, I received one from you addressed to me, registered. My God! It contained the saddest news; what struck me was not so much hearing [what] the Sacred Congregation had decided about the Rule as reading that he who was the true founder is being removed.1 He, I can assure you, is everything to our Institute; if good works have been done, he alone was everything in them.

2. May God's will be done upon our heads, and I, a wretched creature, with my head to the ground, adore all his dispositions and submit to the will of the Church; with the bitterest grief I accept everything.2

3. My health — these grievous sorrows are rushing me towards eternal rest — and my only consolation was to leave the Institute in the arms of its founder, who did and suffered so much for it. God wills this too, and his poor servant adores his divine will with all her soul.

4. This morning I at once sent your letter to the Bishop through the Superior, as I have been gripped by high fever and convulsions since yesterday and can only now hold the pen with difficulty. He sent word that so far he has received nothing from Rome and has no one to give me who could advise me;3 and I have no one I can confide in; if Your Most Reverend Excellency would allow me to come to Rome, I would confide everything to you alone, and the observations could be made better and I could have your advice.4

5. To withdraw the Rule from all the Houses, I at once arranged for letters to be written asking that they all be sent to me in Piacenza, and that those in Ferrara all be handed to the Vicar, as Your Most Reverend Excellency wrote to me.5

6. So I await a letter from you, or a telegram calling me, and on the wings of Providence I will come at once. I would have left immediately, but since I have people staying with us, including the young woman I wrote to you about yesterday, everything holds me back;6 but most of all my health.

7. I have no one to confide a word to except Your Most Reverend Excellency. Allow me to come, and do not deny me your help, nor that of His Eminence, in whom I have placed all my hope.7

8. Humbled at His Eminence's feet, I implore the Apostolic Blessing, and may Your Excellency always keep me supplied with yours, which I need desperately; I add no more, hoping to tell you everything in person, including what you ask me about the Institute;8 and commending myself, unworthy as I am, to your prayers, I remain with every esteem and respect Your Most Reverend Excellency's most humble Sr. A. MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

She realises she is being importunate, but wanting the poor house to get going and grow strong on the way of charity, she asks charity for the poor in their care. God the Father will reward her.1

Most Illustrious Marchioness,

1. Forgive me! I am afraid I realise I am being importunate, but let us hope in the good God that this poor House too will emerge from its poverty and be able to run freely; but being so poor and having only Your Ladyship to help us — a good Mother of charity — in these straits I have come knocking at your noble heart, which [is] all charity for the poor.2

2. So please forgive me again; I thank you infinitely, and God the Father will reward you for all you do and repay it a hundredfold; and we wretches will never cease to pray, as we do daily for Your Ladyship, that you may be granted all you desire.

Believe me, with every esteem and respect, Your Ladyship's most humble Sr. A. M. R. G.

She thanks him for what he told her about the postulant Maddalena. She hopes the young woman will soon take the veil of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

Very Reverend Rector,

1. I cannot find words enough to thank Your Reverence for the great kindness and charity you showed in sending me that little sheet, which contained so much for me and was no small consolation, telling me about the character of that angel Maddalena;1 my gratitude to Your Reverence is such that it will never fade, and in my very feeble prayers I shall not cease to remember you, as I earnestly beg Your Reverence to remember this wretch, who needs it so much, before God.

2. I hope soon to see our Maddalena clothed, and if nothing else intervenes she will take the veil of the Daughters of Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate, on the 10th of next month.2 On that day, Your Reverence, do not forget to pray for us and bless us, as I beg you to do, while I remain with every esteem and respect Your Reverence's

most humble Sr. ANNA M. R. G.

She gives instructions for the house in Via della Morte. She should have the girls pray, take care of herself and keep up her courage. She should tell a girl's uncle and aunt to come and fetch her. She may open letters addressed to the Mother and forward only those needing a reply. She should give news of the Father without naming him: she will say "that person".

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Our daughter for eternity

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I have received a letter from you enclosing one from Nizza, and I can't understand what you tell me about the Father, or rather about his confreres, when the Bishop has said nothing yet. Let us leave everything to God the Father.1

2. My dear, this morning you will have received a letter from Sr. A. Vincenza telling you to send Assunta away at once; I hope you will do it well; tell the one at the Morte that, for charity's sake, I want neither the nuns nor the girl to go out, and that she is to depend in everything on the Main House.2

3. If the Father could write her a line, try to get him to do so with a good scolding.

4. Tell the girls to pray; if God grants me the grace I am asking for, I will give them a lovely present on my return that will please them.

5. You, my dear, take care of yourself, for charity's sake; take courage. My [dear], so many troubles, so many woes! Only my God can remedy them.

6. Listen, send for Giovanna's uncle and aunt and tell them she cannot be placed in the hostel, but there are the Sisters of the Good Shepherd.3 She no longer wants to stay at S. P. D'Arena, and in conscience we cannot keep her, since she scandalises the others.

7. I give you permission to open all letters that come for me and keep them confidential once read. If you see anything I must reply to, send them to me; otherwise keep them, and I will see them when I return. If the Father can continue reading them, then he is enough. Do as before.

8. Listen, did you open the letter from the Superior in Genoa? Tell me, was the money order inside? Tomorrow, when we reach Rome, you will have my address; meanwhile send letters addressed to Father Agostino.

9. For now tell me something more about the Father without naming him. Write «that person».4

10. My dear, stand firm; the devil has thrown a ball, but our God is mighty. Keep me informed of that Person's health.

11. About Maria I can tell you nothing, because I needed to speak to her alone, and besides I took the papers away by mistake.5 Tonight I stop at Foligno.

Goodbye; courage, my dear; strength, for much is needed. God bless you; I am yours for eternity

affectionate MOTHER ROSA

-

She is in the most painful distress over the troubles of her benefactress in Ferrara. She turned to Rosa, who told her to pray and have others pray. She also asks prayers for the approval of the Rule, for which she has had to go to Rome. She should write to her.

My dear friend in Jesus,

1. In the most painful distress, being with the lady in Ferrara and seeing her so tormented by such cruel troubles.1 After she founded the work, my dear, I turned to Rosa; she tells me to ask you and tell you to have prayers said and to pray, and to tell me something: will she soon be consoled? Will that heir of hers who is persecuting her stop harassing her? Will she be happy?2

2. I am going to Rome for our Rule; pray and have others pray.3

3. Write to me at once, by Rosa's order, at my address: Father Agostino, Superior of the Minims of S. Francesco ai Monti, to be handed to Rosa Gattorno, Rome. This is the third time I have written to you and I have never had news from you; answer me; if it is true that it was Rosa, you will answer at once.4

I am your

Affectionate ROSA G.

4. P.S. I am in Rome. Here is the great tribulation you had foretold; I want to know whether it will end soon, yes or no;

what do you say? Answer me at once;5 my address is no longer the one I gave above, but put this: Rosa Gattorno,

c/o the Trevigiani sisters, No. 30 Via della Sapienza.

She may get help from the secretary for external matters; he is an excellent person. She should take courage. The Mother has great strength of spirit and adores God's will in peace.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My dear daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Today is my first [day] in Rome. You will have heard from Sr. A. Vincenza what an unhappy journey we had. You mention the Secretary. Listen, my dear daughter, I wouldn't know what to tell you; commend yourself to Saint Anne and then do what you feel inspired to do. The Secretary is a very good person and for external matters he is everything and very capable, so tell him to see to it. What if the paper he mentions were the Vernengo one?1

2. I think it would be best to wait for my return, which I hope, from what I see, will be very soon.2

3. For pity's sake don't lose courage; be strong; I am now a Hercules of strength — in spirit, that is, for I have no moral strength left; but if you could see how calm I am, adoring God's decrees, ready in everything to do the will of God the Father.3

4. I hear about Sr. A. Assunta; very well, don't send her away; keep her.4

5. Send this letter to Carlotta;5 if any come from Alessandro, I want them. I hope you will receive tomorrow the one Sr. A. Vincenza sent you unstamped.

6. Believe me, my daughter, I have not yet written to anyone; only you have seen my handwriting. I must close because it is late and I want to say my prayers, which I still have to say in full. Goodbye, my dear; I urge you: courage!

God bless you and all the girls, and believe me your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

She hopes to finish soon, but will not be able to go to Piacenza, only to Ferrara. She has had the Rome address sent to all the Houses. If she has obtained the railway fare reduction, she should let her know quickly. She should ask the Secretary for the Vernengo sisters' document.1

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Today after lunch I received your letter telling me so many things. I am glad to hear you have received my letters.

2. Listen, my dear, I am almost done; I have finished everything. I hope Thursday will be the last audience with the Cardinal, Wednesday with the Holy Father, and on Thursday evening, if you have seen to the tickets, I can return; but I am going to Ferrara by order of my superiors and will stay about 15 days.2

3. I can't write, because [I am] very afraid for the letters. Don't trust anyone; I long to hear whether you received my letter in which I spoke of myself.3

4. As for the teacher, do as that Person told you. After the storm comes fair weather — all the more when it comes with hail.

5. I have received the trunk; all is well; thank you for everything. God bless you; for the money go with Sr. A. Gesuina, so that you can pay for the bread.4

6. Mystery — everything around us. I am glad you have not yet received anything; let us hope St Joseph will set everything right. I pray to this great saint, but my prayers are worth nothing. You can't imagine how eagerly I await your letters; I would like one every day, always telling me something. You mention Giovanna; I think they should go and fetch her themselves.5

7. As for the address, I have had all the houses informed; so on Thursday at the latest I leave for Ferrara. If you have obtained the half fare, you could have it sent to the ticket office at the station by telegram, and I will do the same; I will let you know when I leave.6 Meanwhile, act accordingly: don't write to me any more. For the rest, do as you think best. As for the Vernengo paper, tell the Secretary to draw it up and then send it, and have him write asking them to send the paper I asked for about the properties on which their dowry is secured; that is what you must have him say.7 It is late and I don't feel very well. I am your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA. God bless you together with all the others.

She has received the mortal blow: she will have to compile the Rule herself. After the audience with the Holy Father she will go to Ferrara. She is resigned to God's will in this martyrdom, which she expects to last long. She should send the application for the reduced train fare and send her the ticket for her journey.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My dear daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Today I received your letter with the key of the trunk, and I hear you still know nothing; but it is not so for this poor Mother of yours; yesterday and this morning I thought I would go mad; the pain was killing me; God alone can understand it.

2. Yesterday at one o'clock they dealt me the mortal blow: deprived of everything, I may no longer write to that person; I am required to compile the Rule under the direction of the Bishop of Ferrara,1 whom I saw this morning; he leaves for Ferrara on Sunday, and if God grants me the audience on Sunday, I too will leave on Monday the 4th of next week.

3. I am sorry too that you have not yet received the money order from the Delegate Serafina;2 I really don't know what to say; I would be in favour of removing the letter box and letting the postman bring the letters; meanwhile it seems it makes no difference, and you can complain to the post office, or rather speak to the Secretary.3

4. My dear, on my return I am going to Ferrara, then, to rearrange the Rule. I hope to be quick, because... I can't say everything. God's will be done!

5. If you see that person, tell him I hope I have found out everything;4 I think this martyrdom is crueller than the guillotine, and those who are hanged [suffer] less, because what they feel is that moment of the noose round their neck, but in an hour it is all over; whereas this — God knows how long it will last.

6. The Bishop of Genoa is worse and worse towards us; what can we do?5 Adore God's mighty hand, which is pleased to let Cepinetto target us; but it will not always be so, for our Eternal Father will drive this monster away and in his mercy give us peace.

7. Listen, my dear, before leaving I didn't think to check where to apply for half fare on journeys to Rome.6 Listen, the paper the Prefect gave me is in the cupboard; ask Merli7 what you should do. For charity's sake, don't let the paper get lost; try to be quick; I am waiting, because meanwhile it is something to have half fare.

8. As for Sr. A. Assunta, leave everything as it is, then; may it be for the best. You tell me nothing about Sr. A. Concetta: whether she sent you the paper, whether they are doing what we planned for them.8

9. My head is so much in the clouds that I can't remember anything, but tomorrow I will write to them that if they are ready they should come, and that we should first draw up the paper the Secretary will send them. That done, let them come to Piacenza, where I hope to be by Easter.9

10. My dear, do you see how many humiliations? This one too — what can we do! If every door is closing,10 we must press on by the sweat of blood as long as we have a drop of it in our veins. I am waiting for the ticket.

11. I want to know whether that person ever sent the letter you mention, which he wanted you to stamp; I have received nothing. What can have happened? For charity's sake, I would not want it to be lost; did it stay in Bologna?

12. Write to me; I shall not leave until I have the ticket you will send. The day before I leave I will telegraph you. As for the girls, do whatever you think; it will always be well done.

Goodbye; the Lord bless you; believe me always your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

She has acted truly well. If the Countess comes to Ferrara, she should visit her and, if she would like it, bring the Sisters too. She should pray and have others pray to St Joseph for providence and to Saint Anne for what is worrying her.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

My good Superior

[Letter of Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino, to which the Mother adds:]

1. Yes, my daughter,1 God bless you; you have truly acted like someone inspired; go on doing as you write.

2. I have just received your letter; all is well; go to the Countess at once if she comes to Ferrara; don't go to Bologna any more, but as soon as you hear she has arrived go and visit her, and if you see it pleases her, tell her that her daughters long to see her; if she allows, I will bring them to her two at a time; they are eager to see her.

3. I hope you have written to her, as I had Sr. A. Vincenza tell you.

4. For charity's sake, have them pray; begin the month of St Joseph, and have the girls in school do it too, so that this Saint may grant, or rather obtain for us, the grace we ask2 and providence for our houses. I fear that by Easter we shall have to think about this for here too.3

5. Dear daughter, what torments there are in this world! Worse than martyrdom: this one is prolonged and no one knows when it will end; God alone can know.

6. Please have the community say, until further notice, 9 Hail Marys to Saint Anne for the nine [months] she carried the child Mary in her womb. We have nothing but prayers, and these will move God's heart, and we shall have a little peace.

7. So I will soon be with you, and for a long time. Goodbye, so that I can post this.4 Greet all the Sisters for me. God bless them all.

Goodbye; I bless you. I am ever your affectionate

MOTHER ROSA

From Rome she commends to her the poor House in Piacenza. In the audience with the Holy Father she will ask a blessing for her and her brothers. She will leave Rome for Ferrara.

A.M.F.

Most Illustrious Countess,

1. It would have been my duty to write to you as soon as I reached Rome, but I suffered so much on the journey that I could not do so until now. I spoke to Father Agostino about that person, but he knows nothing; I think he has left Rome.1

2. Troubles and the cruellest tribulations overwhelm us; only God and Saint Anne can help us. Most Illustrious Countess, do not forget the poor House there. On Monday I hope to have the audience with the Holy Father, and I will not forget to ask [a blessing] for you and your Noble brothers.2

3. On Saturday next week I leave Rome for Ferrara. If you have any commission for me, I shall be glad to serve you.3

4. In person I will tell you so many things that you could never imagine so many sad things could happen in an Age of anguish like ours.4

Many greetings to your Most Illustrious Brothers and to the very Reverend Father Cirillo,5 and believe me Your Ladyship's

most humble Sr. ANNA MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

She tells her that Mgr Vitelleschi has set the matter well on its way. She gives news of Fr Giuseppe Manfredini's health. She will leave Rome and hopes to see her again in Bologna or Ferrara. She tells her of a widow's prophecy about the Pope.

My beloved Sister,

1. As soon as I am on my feet I set about writing to you to ask your forgiveness and mercy; you well knew that I always told you: believe me, I am nothing but the world's leftover, good for nothing but doing everything badly. Everything I say I take from experience and from the little I can know in a material way; for the rest, a most wretched creature approaching eternity with great strides.1

2. Today everything was concluded for us. Mgr Vitelleschi arranged everything very well, and God's Work has made great progress.2 The anguish and pains this most wretched creature suffered — may God accept them for my benefactress and true foundress of this poor Order.3

3. On Monday I shall have the audience — a private one, I hope; the first thing I shall say to His Holiness will be to ask him to bless our Mother, our foundress.4

4. I have not yet seen Father Manfredini,5 because he was better and put himself under Homeopathic treatment, and relapsed; yesterday Mgr Mariano came to see me and said he had seen him, that those Homeopathic doctors had been dismissed, and he seems a little better; but his abdomen is still swollen.

5. Today I spoke with Cav. Vaciali, who said he will write to you tomorrow with many details.6 I hope next Thursday to be back. If I do not have the joy of seeing you and handing everything over in Bologna, I shall be at your feet in Ferrara, my lady — let me put it so, for I find the term very apt.

6. If times were different and you were not so set against prophecies, I would tell you a little about the woman who prophesied what she said to that dear soul, the Count.7 She is a widow; this is how I heard: Father Agostino knows a noble family, the Mas.8, now in Rome with his Lady, who come expressly to visit this holy Widow, who lives in a village near Naples; they had an audience with the Holy Father and told him everything — that he should leave — and the Marchioness said: yes, we do not want him to stay in the Vatican; she says that by June everything would be over, a great scourge in Rome and Paris, and then many other things.9

7. Forgive me, for pity's sake; tomorrow everything in Father Manfredini's Room will be handed to me. Today I received a letter from Signor Mirandola with bad news of your health; for the love of God, have someone write to me, since I am no longer worthy of your handwriting. Patience! For my infamies everything is too little. If it is not too much trouble, please give my warm greetings to Ninetta and Signor Mirandola,10 and receive an embrace in the Heart of Jesus, where I remain your

most affectionate SISTER R.11 G.12

Next week the Parish Priest of Nizza will arrive with two postulants. She will send her the silk and other items to give to benefactors. She should have the cups numbered, have the chimney hood repaired, and the kitchen whitewashed and thoroughly cleaned.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

My blessed daughter,

1. I cannot understand your silence; it makes me fear for your health. Only today am I on my feet, and God knows how I am, but always glad to be able to suffer a little to atone for my enormous misdeeds, which have no equal.

2. Today I hear from Nizza that next week the Parish Priest will come with the two postulants;1 one is bringing only 150 F. for now and will give the rest as soon as possible. I hope the house will be in order; put these two postulants upstairs.

3. I am very sorry about Sr. A. Fortunata; she must take care of herself.2

4. I want you to buy me the silk for Maria,3 the finest, sample enclosed; indeed, if it were a strand finer it would be better. Then I will send you this and you will hand it over. I am waiting to send you that skein of ugly silk, because I hope to put it in a box I will ship you containing two caps, one for Merli and the other for lanesae(?), and then you will see what seems best.4

5. Make the cup with No. 50; the Superior of S. P. D'Arena gave it to Sr. A. Benvenuta, one of her postulants; so you can go by that and no longer send No. 94. Send 91, 92, 93: 91 and 92 to Genoa and 93 to S. P. D'Arena.5

6. Merli wrote to me that the Town Council will send you 200 F. at the beginning of this month. You must also collect Sr. A. Eugenia's 375 F.;6 try to pay the miller and something for the pasta; if you think it best to buy a little wheat for the girls, do as you think.

7. I urge you to keep the girls in order; they are truly a heavy cross.

8. Please tell the Sisters at the Morte about the novena to the Eternal Father, even if they have to begin it later.7

9. I also let you know that Sr. A. Apanasia's number is 82; but don't send her a cup — keep it with you, and the others too, so they avoid breaking them.8 That is all for now.

10. One more thing: show the kitchen to the mason and tell him I want him to cure the smoke, because I want it gone; or let him make the chimney hood bigger, so that it covers all the stoves and draws the smoke away, because now you have it whitewashed and in two days it will be black again; once the smoke is gone, have the kitchen whitewashed too, and with its coppers hanging up9 it will look better and be cleaner.

11. The workroom with its fanchelen10 and all the rest, closed; the postulants' refectory — if you could have it repaired a little; or else, you know, it seems to me that when needed the door should be shut so that it is not damaged; so whenever it seems [right] to close it, it is closed.11

12. Another thing: how are the flowers? Have the trees taken? The portress's will be lovely; tell her I was very pleased with her labours and that the Holy Mother will keep her alive for many years; she must not overwork. Let her have Giovanni water them.12

Goodbye, my dear daughter; take care of yourself. I await your letters and am

your affectionate MOTHER ROSA

What happened regarding that person and the Rule was caused by his rigidity and his exalted doctrine. It is the general view that she must look after herself and take care. Everything is entrusted to her; the Institute survives only because she is there. What reasons — she who has never done anything and can do nothing! She should accompany the Sister to settle a financial matter. The Bishop of Piacenza has been informed.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My dear daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I have received yours and cannot understand that you have not received my letter, not even the one containing a letter for that person, which was stamped.1 For charity's sake, tell me at once whether you have received it.

2. As for that person and all that happened, it is all down to rigidity and his exalted doctrine, but more to the rigidity he showed me, for it is believed he treated me like a beast and kept me like a beast of burden. That is the whole of it; but I am glad I came, and today I am going to the Holy Office.2 On Monday I shall have the private audience with the Holy Father and leave at once for Ferrara.

3. The general view is that I ought to look after myself and take more care until the Institute is firmly established, and they declared that they are leaving everything as it is because I am still alive — only, only that! Otherwise they would have made a bundle of it. My God! What reasons — I who have never done anything and can do nothing; I, truly a donkey, less than that; what do you say, my daughter?3

4. Saint Anne, my Mother, help me! Last night and the night before I thought I would lose my mind, I was so agitated; I have no one to whom I can say a word!

5. Have that Person read this letter of mine; I am forbidden to communicate with him. Mystery! Mystery!4

6. You tell me about Sr. A. Gesuina; yes, go with her for a day, it is better; I think there are Sisters of Charity in that town, or you can stay at her aunt's house for a day; so you hear everything, do everything, finish it off, and spend less.5 They will be useful to you; I am worried about the 200 F. from the Delegate in Genoa.6

7. You also ask me about the Sacred Heart.7 Do whatever you think, my dear daughter; what can I tell you, here in the midst of the most dreadful battles? They know everything. Enough; tomorrow I will write again. In haste, your

Affectionate MOTHER

Pray Pray Pray, or else...

8. P.S. Sr. A. Vincenza is writing to the Bishop of Piacenza. I receive everything from God's hands. Only one thing pains me: my boys. Giggino's letter knocked me flat.8 Wretched me,

what have I done?

She reports what she has done in Rome concerning the new Rule and the decisions on it communicated to her by Mgr Salvatore Vitelleschi. She has already made arrangements with Mgr Giordani. She will go to Ferrara, where he will help her compile the Rule.

Your Most Reverend Excellency,

1. As is my duty, I inform Your Most Reverend Excellency that I did not reach Rome from Bologna until the evening of the 27th of last month.

2. I spoke at once with His Eminence Cardinal Vannicelli, who directed me to Mgr Vitelleschi;1 this is what that Holy Prelate told me: that for the reform of the Rule2 I have been entrusted to His Excellency Mgr Giordani, Bishop of Ferrara, and that His Holiness wishes this Institute, which does so much good, to be consolidated so that it may spread and bear greater fruit: these are Mgr Vitelleschi's words.

3. I have already spoken with His Excellency Bishop Giordani. He received me with indescribable charity, which calmed my spirit a little. He leaves for Ferrara on Sunday, and as soon as I have had the audience with the Holy Father I shall join him.3

4. Once in Ferrara, I shall make it my duty to keep Your Excellency informed, for you have done so much good to the poor Daughters of Saint Anne; I have always found in Your Excellency a Father, a Shepherd, a comfort in my many anxieties, which I can never forget.

Humbly at your Feet, I implore your Fatherly blessing, and remain with all esteem and veneration Your Most Reverend Excellency's most humble Sr. A. MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

She has had the audience with the Holy Father and felt comforted. She has spoken with others about the Rule and found out the points being contested. She will tell her everything in person. Sr. A. Vincenza says she is pestered because people think her so holy that she fears they will cut up her habit for relics. Both had a nasty adventure while driving in a carriage to see Monsignor.1

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter for ever

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Today I had the private audience. I spoke with the Holy Father. On seeing me he laughed several times: "Ah! Ah! the Daughters of Saint Anne, the Daughters of Saint Anne". He pressed my hand and I was able to tell him everything. Holding his hand I pleaded with him; in short, I was very happy, as the first time, perhaps more.2 I won't write you what, because I am always afraid.3

2. Afterwards we went to see other people, but I got such a headache I thought I would die. Now, barely recovered, I write to you in my own [hand], as I always do. I am waiting for the money order and the paper, which I have not yet received; otherwise I would leave.

3. So: Daughters of Saint Anne, but don't say Mother of the Immaculate.4 Silence, for charity's sake! Saint Anne, Daughters of Saint Anne; I have found out everything, I know everything. Be of good heart. Have that person read this letter. The storm is about to calm down.

4. I learn from a letter of the good Marchioness Anguissola that she has sent you 150 F.5 Blessed be God.

5. I have bought a little something for everyone, but I certainly shan't come before the end of the month. I hope you received my letter yesterday with one inside for that person. I thought I would leave tomorrow, but I still have many visits to make. With God the Father's help I hope to be ready on Friday, provided I don't fare as today, when I had to be taken home because I felt so ill.

6. Sr. A. Vincenza is here and tells me she wishes everyone thought her wicked, to be spared so much bother; that she fears they will cut up her habit into so many relics; she said it in all seriousness. I laughed so convulsively that my head even aches.6

7. The hood is all ruffled, and how... do you understand me? does the reader understand?...7

8. We are really well. What dear creatures! Two sisters alone8 and...

9. Have they brought you the oil for St Joseph? Keep his lamp lit. Have them pray; remember that on Saturday I shall be travelling. God grant me a good journey.

10. My dear daughter, you can tell this.9 Some days ago we were in a carriage. What can you do? Cepinello really wants me dead. A coachman — the Lord knows who he was — anyway, he tried to kill us: three times he drove us against the wall; the third time we saw ourselves dead. Everyone came out; the horse, jammed on the bit, was going belly to the ground. When God willed, there were so many people that he had to stop a little, and I took the chance and jumped out. So did Sr. A. Vincenza. My God, what a fright! We were more dead than alive all day. People wanted to give us something to drink.

11. Without a word we went to Monsignor's, since we were close by. Sr. A. Vincenza was tugging at the coachman's coat with all her strength like a woman in despair. He would not budge. Sr. A. Vincenza was afraid because she had not been to confession; fear made her tear the poor coachman's frock coat.10 When you see how she did it, the scene turns from tragic to lyrical. Afterwards one laughs, but being there is awful. I am your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

She sends her a letter to be handed to Fr Tornatore. The letter is continued and signed by her secretary, Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino.1

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter for ever

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Today I received yours with two lines from that person inside. Tell him, for charity's sake, that if he is going to write like that he should not write to me.2 I shall soon be there. Listen: give him at once the enclosed letter; it is for that person. I shall be (?) on my feet; you misunderstood my letter; for charity's sake, read it carefully. Tomorrow I go to the Holy Father and have the private audience; pray to St Joseph [...].3

She tells her the departure is set for the next day and gives the itinerary of the journeys that follow. She may hand the girl who wants to leave over to her relatives and settle the accounts. She should decide what needs doing in the house. The Religious should pray, be cheerful, speak to no one of the community's problems and pay no heed to others' gossip.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

My daughter for ever,

1. Last night I received your telegram, and during the day I had received the money, 150 F., which I went to collect from the Post Office myself; the day before, the paper.1

2. God willing, I leave tomorrow, Sunday, at 9 in the morning, having been unable to leave earlier because I still had to speak with a Monsignor; so tomorrow at 6 and a few minutes I shall be in Florence, where I stop and sleep. In the morning I leave again for Bologna, where I stop just one hour to hand the Countess a few small things; then straight on to Ferrara, where I shall stay until next Saturday, and then at once to Piacenza for only 1 day and then straight to Genoa, where there are matters of great importance. You will hear in person.

3. You ask me about Carolina; you can tell her they should come with the money, and you will hand over her rags, which are nothing but old tatters she had, and certain things even the Mother had to make for her. Indeed, let them come, and insist that they bring you the money; get all her rags ready; only for the iron bed they gave me 20 F., and I understood this was so that she could be lent one, because it seems to me that little can be had for 20 F.; and tell them that for two years I gave her no straw mattress, only an old one, and I had to give her one belonging to the community; and if I were to count everything, certainly it would be owed to me,2 but one can see they want to take advantage, because we are religious, and this is the world's payment; but since we work for God, He will take care of everything.

4. I hope you will go on Gesuina's behalf,3 which truly seems to me a real torment. We are scourged on every side. Piacenza! Piacenza! You will weep for your scourges on innocent backs; God grant you do not pay the debt with your sweat. If you struck the innocent, know that one day they will be your glory...!!4

5. You ask about rotas for the laundry. My daughter, do as you think; you judge these things better, for I have so much on my mind that I wouldn't know what to tell you. For Easter nothing will be done; let all be mute, silence on every side. Tell all the Religious to pray and pay no attention to gossip, not to answer; so no one will know anything.5

6. Within your own house be cheerful; say not a syllable to anyone; perfect silence.

7. We sent the trunk straight to Piacenza. Greet all the Sisters for me, and receive an embrace from your most affectionate Mother, who calls herself yours as she blesses you with all the others and remains your

Poor MOTHER ROSA

She asks his permission to be absent from Ferrara, as she must go to Genoa on business.

Your Most Reverend Excellency,

1. I reached Ferrara only last night, and this morning, as was my duty, I hastened to Your feet to hear whatever Your Excellency might kindly command me.1 But unfortunately Your Excellency had left for the country barely a quarter of an hour before.

2. Were Your residence nearer and my poor health allowed it, I would gladly have come to do my duty; but since this is impossible, I take up my pen to ask Your Apostolic blessing and at the same time permission to leave next Monday, the 18th of this month, as I must go to Genoa on business; I would return to Ferrara whenever Your Most Reverend Excellency is free to hear me.

3. Impart Your Apostolic blessing to one who asks it again, as I remain Your Most Reverend Excellency's most humble Sr. ANNA MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

She thanks him for his protection, kindness and fatherly comfort in her sorrows. Her gratitude and her Daughters' becomes a prayer of thanksgiving to God for the gift of so great and charitable a Protector. She has already called on Bishop Giordani.

Your Most Reverend Eminence,

1. My small capacity and mental limitation1 do not allow me to set down in vivid characters all that would be needed to express eloquently the gratitude my soul feels towards Your Most Reverend Eminence. The protection, the loving welcome given me when, a poor little woman, I came to Your feet: in Your Eminence I found every comfort, every relief, every support in my most painful anguish.

2. Duty obliges me, and gladness urges me above all, as soon as I have stopped — I have been in Ferrara since yesterday — to tell You with all my heart and in the name of the whole Institute that we shall keep an eternal memory of it and thank the Most High for giving us so great and charitable a Protector.

3. Today I went to His Excellency Bishop Giordani to receive his Apostolic blessing, but did not find him, as he had left for the country.2

4. I found this little Community cheerful amid its hardships and full of trust in God and in Your Most Reverend Eminence, at Whose Feet all prostrate themselves imploring Your Apostolic blessing, while with the deepest veneration I sign myself Your Most Reverend Eminence's most humble Servant Sr. A. MARIA

ROSA GATTORNO

Grateful for his kindness and help at a time of such sadness, she expresses her thanks. She is already in Ferrara to compile the Rule. She will go to Genoa. If he writes to the Archbishop of Genoa, would he add a word of recommendation for the Houses of the Daughters of Saint Anne in that Diocese.

Your Most Reverend Excellency,

1. The great charity and kindness with which Your Excellency received and protected me at a time of such sadness are so imprinted on me that I have made vows of gratitude to my God, that He may fill You with graces and repay You a hundredfold for all You have done and are doing for our poor Institute. This most wretched servant of the Lord, together with all our communities, will raise special prayers every day to the Most High for Your preservation.

2. I have been in Ferrara since last night; I have not yet spoken to His Excellency Mgr Giordani, who is at his country house.1 I shall leave for Genoa on Thursday the 21st of this month.

3. If Your Most Reverend Excellency writes to Archbishop Magnasco,2 I beg You to add a word of recommendation for our poor Houses in his Diocese, knowing that one word from You will suffice to obtain every good.

4. Please grant Your Apostolic blessing on all the Daughters of Saint Anne and especially on the one who needs it most and who bows respectfully at Your Feet, remaining Your Most Reverend Excellency's

most humble Sr. ANNA MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

She answers two questions with the necessary directions. Mgr Giordani has gone to the country. Early next week she will go to Piacenza and then to Genoa. The Countess no longer gives the monthly subsidy. She will tell the Sisters of the House in Via della Morte to be cheerful, for she will soon be with them. She regrets what is being said about Father Tornatore and the Institute. In constant work and suffering she is cheerful and resigned. She should pray and have others pray to St Joseph. Be cheerful.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My dear daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Today I received your letter announcing the death of the Pagani girl. Let us bless the Lord who took her to himself; believe me, living might perhaps have been bad for her; likewise Delfina is going to enjoy what she would surely lose if she stayed down here in this land of exile.1

2. You ask me about Carolina's mattress. Well, send it, I tell you, without having it washed; they must see to that.2

3. As for going to teach catechism in the Paganina church, it would be good to speak to that person and have him tell us what he thinks. I would be inclined to send them on condition that they always teach it themselves and no one else interferes.3

4. Here is the second thing you ask me; but have that person read this letter. Yesterday I went to Mgr Giordani, Bishop of Philadelphia, but he had left for the country, so last night I wrote to him;4 today they took it to him, and I shall hear whether he is coming or waiting for me to come again.

5. In any case, I leave on Monday and shall be in Piacenza at 6 in the afternoon; come and fetch me — let me know whether you have received this — and on Thursday at 11.30 I must be in Genoa. What travelling, my God!

6. Here all is well, except that yesterday I received the verdict that the Countess will no longer give anything, and everything rests on the shoulders of providence.5 What worries, my God! I feel my head will no longer stay in place; I try to shut it in God's heart, but even there it wanders.

7. Tell the Sisters at the Morte6 to be cheerful, for I shall soon be with them and will go to see them.

8. You tell me what the Bishop said to you about that person. Certainly, if he had kept coming, no one would have said anything and the city would know nothing; but if we let it be noticed, everyone gets to know our affairs; and then we must take care to confide in no one, for what happened came not from the accounts of Sr. A. Vincenza and this Delegate, but from what he said to the Copucio(?).7

9. I heard things such that, were it not for the hand of God holding me up, I felt my chest would be strangled with grief. To listen, everyone is a friend, but then they use it as they please. Patience! The day of death will remedy so many of my troubles. Alone on earth, it is torment for me. God alone sustains and governs me.

10. Courage, daughter, for dying on the cross needs strength and resignation. I have no rest day or night, always at the desk writing from morning to evening, worries upon worries, labours upon labours; everywhere I find cruel thorns, but always cheerful and always resigned; so my Jesus teaches me.

11. Signor Liberali is hearing confessions; a moment ago he sent word that the Superior is coming! I hope you have received the box. Don't open it until I come; I'll open it myself. I'll tell you many things in person.

12. What is St Joseph doing? Is he bringing providence? Shout loudly, for he is old, and so, being a little — you understand me... — one must8 shout; that is why he doesn't hear me, as I have little voice. Dear

Saint, I hope for much in this month of his — if only he would convert the Marchioness for us! Goodbye; greet everyone for me, and you in particular. God bless you and give you strength, patience, resignation and peace.

I am all yours, affectionate MOTHER ROSA. Greet that person for me.

13. Cheer up, for I hope cepinetto will break his nose on some wall and we shall be rid of him.9

14. I am well, and as you will learn from this, I shall be with you on Monday; meanwhile accept the girl. Have this read, or rather read it yourself, to the house at the Morte.10 I am very sorry about your news. I am astonished that the Superior had the nerve to give such permission to go to the cathedral for the sermon. My God! What your heart must have suffered! So, for charity's sake, let this Superior never again give such permissions.

15. Pray and humble yourselves. You daughters of the Morte,11 write to your Mother, who is waiting for your letters, and tell me how you are and what is happening with the Casa del Verme; I will provide you with tickets and whatever you need; I don't say all of you should write, but one for all, as I have much to do and it would be too tiring for me; besides, on Monday I shall be with you and will come at once to see you at the Morte.

16. You, my dear Franceschina, be cheerful, and you will see how many lovely things I have brought you. You will hear how our Jesus knew how to heal our wounds.

17. I am sending you the key of the trunk so you can collect it from the station, but don't open it until I come. Listen, it would be best for you to fetch it from the station yourself, so you can be sure nothing goes missing, as there are so many lovely things in it that tempt people.

[MOTHER ROSA]

To settle a known matter she had better entrust it to the Secretary's son. She will inform the Secretary. She should tell "that person" to go to the Palazzo Dal Verme; she must speak to him. She will be in Piacenza on Monday at 6 p.m.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Today I received your letter about that person. You see whether it was true. Well, let us leave everything in God's hands; this good Father does everything for our good.

2. Listen, for Gesuina I would be in favour of sending the Secretary's son, because a thousand thoughts came to me that I will tell you in person.1 I am having the Secretary written to at this moment.2 Be calm, we will do everything. Courage, daughter; the sorrows are many, so trust and strength must be as great.

3. Sr. A. Concetta will send you a paper; take it to the Secretary.3 He is fully informed, including the day I arrive.

4. Tell that person that I cannot go to S. Lazzaro; if he thinks fit to come to the house for a moment — indeed he may come. The reason I cannot go I will tell him in person.

5. I have a world of things to make you laugh; cepinetto laughs because he makes us despair and gets up to his tricks because St Michael the Archangel let him escape, but we must make the fig at him and laugh more than he does.4

6. Now listen, it would have been good if you had answered what you write about the Parish Priest; you should have said: Father, if Providence provides for the others, it would provide for those poor boys too.

7. Don't write to me any more, because on Monday I shall be with you at 6 in the evening;5 come to the station. I hope that person will be able to come,

but if not, God's will be done in all things. Goodbye; in haste, your

Affectionate [MOTHER ROSA]. Greet everyone and that person for me. God bless you; I am yours

8. P.S. I warn you not to send the globe to the

Morte until I come; for charity's sake, they will certainly break it.6 If you have already sent it, have Sr. A. of the

Good Shepherd fetch it back; put it at the far end of the guest quarters, where no one goes, and keep it covered. Keep the books with you too; when I come we will decide.

She has had a long talk with Mgr Giordani. On returning from Genoa she will set to work. She hopes to see the Constitutions completed and, before she dies, definitively approved. She will write to him from Genoa.

Your Most Reverend Excellency,

1. In the very first free moment I have, I gather my little strength to talk with You, as I have several small things to tell You, and at the same time to let You know that Mgr Giordani came today and we had a long conference; everything was agreed, and on my return from Genoa I hope, with God the Father's help, to be able to arrange everything very well; and You, by Your work, will compile our Constitutions, so that they may be approved before this poor servant of the Lord closes her eyes.1

2. Thank You for the letter addressed to Sr. A. Vincenza which I received yesterday;2 I am at a loss for fitting words to express my gratitude and how deeply I am indebted for Your great kindness. As for the person Your Most Reverend Excellency mentions, I received a letter from her today, and from its contents she seems to be coming round. God grant it, for the good of His work.3

3. When I reach Genoa I will write to tell You how things stand; and that little matter You know of seems, from what I am told, to be all prepared. Kindly present my most heartfelt respects to His Eminence and obtain for me his Apostolic blessing, adding Your own, as I remain Your Most Reverend Excellency's most humble Servant Sr. A. MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

She cannot account for her silence and fears she is ill. She will write to the Sisters of the Community in Via della Morte and to those of the Mother House. She thinks the girl proposed should, given her particular circumstances, be taken in at Genoa. She has been received very coldly by Mgr Magnasco.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I cannot understand why you have not written. I am worried that you are unwell. A thousand thoughts come to me; I am fairly well.

2. Today at 11 I go to the Bishop, and then I will write to that person, so you will hear how it went. My God, how I dread it! At the mere thought of seeing him I feel faint. What feelings!1

3. I hope Merli is back, or rather that he will go there for the money.2

4. How are the Sisters at the Morte? I will write to them as soon as I can, in good ink, next week; you too will have one to read to all the sisters in chapter.3

5. I have just received your letter; I am glad to hear you are fairly well. I also hear all that is happening in that house.

6. As for the girl you mention, the only solution would be for her to settle in this house in Genoa, because in S. P. D'Arena, being too old, and [given] the reason they are putting her away, it is not good for her to go where there are good little girls; so you can tell them that, if they wish, here in Genoa, provided they pay her journey and 50 F. on entry, and 20 a month, always in advance.4

7. My dear, if you knew how Mgr Magnasco received me — it is truly odd: standing, leaning on a support, and he kept me standing the whole time; not even the Pope received me like that. For the love of God, everything is too little.5

8. I hope you received my letter, or rather Sr. A. Vincenza's. I would like a salame for Signora Vernengo and another for Federico, but small ones, otherwise none will be left for us.6

Tomorrow I will write to that person. Goodbye; the Lord bless you. I am your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

In Genoa she called on Mgr Magnasco. She was received with extreme coldness and left standing while she reported on the Institute. She suffered and offered her anguish to the Father. She found the Genoa Houses in good order. With the help of Providence all is well. She has just received a consoling letter from him.

Your Most Reverend Excellency,

1. Allow me to address a word to You to give vent to my poor soul. A few hours ago I again called on Monsignor Magnasco, Archbishop of Genoa, having arrived in his Diocese only a day ago. My God! The way he received me was such that I thought I would faint; I cannot describe the manner in which he spoke to me; what an impression it made on me! My breast was under the anvil, such was my apprehension on hearing it; I said to myself: those Holy Cardinals, those Prelates, who in their humility always received this servant of the Lord with such Charity and kindness, which gave me strength to sustain so many battles; and while I felt myself fainting from having to stand the whole time reporting to him, I was not even told to sit down, though I was truly fainting; indeed I tried to finish quickly so that there would be no scene.

2. Your Most Reverend Excellency knows how much I dislike making the least scene. Patience; at once I made an offering of it to my Eternal Father and, full of resignation and peace, I clung to Jesus.

3. Forgive me if my outpouring is too bold; but to whom can I turn, having no one now but Your Most Reverend Excellency?

I also venture to ask Your advice on how I should proceed in writing to Monsignor Vitelleschi.

4. Here the Houses are doing very well, everything is in order, and Providence too keeps coming. What a consolation: I have just received a letter from You, a true balm for this wretched Servant of Yours.1 May God reward You and fill You with graces.

5. Carlottina, who is here, together with Sr. A. Vincenza, the Superior of this house and the whole Community, ask You to request a special blessing for them from His Eminence, adding Your own, and all prostrate implore from God the grace of a good journey for You.2

May Your blessing descend in a special way on this Your most humble Servant Sr. A. MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

They will talk better about "that person" in person. She had not accepted the postulant mentioned. She urges care over laundry and cleanliness. They must take care to hand over personal linen to Sisters who are transferred. She will send two letters, for the sisters in Via della Morte and at the Mother House respectively. She will stay in Genoa for Easter. She should look after her health. Various instructions for the house.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My Franceschina for ever

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Today I received your letter about that person. Don't think it is so; I don't believe it; I think the order's affairs being settled has changed him. Well, we will talk about this in person.1

2. My dear, these lines I write you I take from my eyes, because I have had to talk all day. I am tired; my stomach aches.

3. I hear too what you say about that postulant. Know that I had already sent her away, telling Signora Scopesi, who had proposed her, that I could not accept her because she had been with the Sisters of Charity, and our Constitutions require this of us.2

4. As for Clotilde, I quite think that, for the money involved, a paper will suffice without having her make a will.3

5. I urge you to have our laundry done after Easter, and the girls' too, if they need it again.4 For charity's sake, watch over cleanliness, and let nothing be wasted.

6. Here they complain that the numbers on the chemises are not those of the sisters who came, and the same with other linen.5 For charity's sake, let the Sisters' things be numbered, and when one has to go elsewhere let her be given them. This is the wardrobe-keeper's job.

7. I hope the money has reached you. I want to make you laugh: as soon as I arrived I had to empty my pocket and was left with only a few pennies.

8. I hope tomorrow to write the letters for the Sisters and will send them to you, one for that house and the other for the Morte.6

9. My dear, I am spending Easter in this little house, which seems to me the only one in which to stay buried,7 as I have no head for attending any services, so many are the tasks of every kind in this work. My God, it is my sins that stifle me. Have them pray; I hope the girls will be happy and pray more fervently.

10. You ask me about the visit to the Holy Sepulchre;8 they could go at times when no one is there, but it will be much better if they do as in other years, when they stayed at home.

11. I hope you received the letter in which I told you about Monsignor's reception of me.9

12. I enclose two lines for you-know-who, but I want them handed to him by you and no longer sent through Giovanni. You know that on Wednesdays he goes to St Joseph's; you can have him called and give it to him, and so save yourself going to S. Lazzaro. I am not writing the address; you know whom it is for.10

13. For charity's sake, take care of yourself, don't overwork, keep calm, for this poor Mother of yours always holds you close in the heart of Jesus; for charity's sake, think of your health; I will send you pills, by tomorrow I hope; take them and you will recover completely. You see, my dear, when we no longer have our health we are good for nothing.

Goodbye; the Lord bless you; believe me always your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

14. God bless all; let them pray. Of Carolina's11 things we kept no record, because she kept them herself, and as everything gets sorted out, she had them given back when she returned; so we never had much of them. It will be good for the girls to stay indoors all day;

it is better, for charity's sake. I wouldn't know what to tell her about dairy foods; let her ask Don Piacenza.12 Let her never refuse any postulant if she does not have 500 F. on entry and 3000 F. dowry; so I mean that whoever wishes may come, whoever doesn't may stay.

Yes, sweets at recreation and coffee; the rest you know;13 if [you have] not yet sent the basket, I would need a crucifix and the rosaries I left.

At last she has had news from the House, four days after her arrival. She had been worried by the silence. She herself had been unable to write for serious health reasons. She addresses all the Sisters, urging trust in their Superiors. Their conduct towards them should be marked by sincerity and simplicity. They should practise mortification, above all of the tongue and of thoughts, and strive to cultivate their vocation and look on high.1

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

Our daughter,

1. Today I received your letter enclosing the Milan programme, as well as the good news from the Mayor and from Grandi.2 Let us bless the Lord that, in these times when poor Religious are so harshly treated, they tolerate the poor Daughters of Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate.

2. I am also very sorry at the sad news of my good daughter Benedetta. Patience! If it so pleases the Lord, let us too savour his pleasure, so that every drink becomes sweet to us, even one made of gall.

3. I was really worried because I had no news of you; today it was 4 days since I left, and I had not a single line from you. You will know why I did not write to you at once; Father will have told you: I could barely put two lines together two days after arriving here, because the journey was truly wretched and the next day brought an even greater strain; I was seized by pains all over my body so dreadful that they made me faint. Today I can barely breathe a little, and still not well.

4. How is the good postulant in charge of the middle girls? For charity's sake, look after her, for she is a miracle; poor thing, seeing her so resigned edified me.

5. Have you sent Sr. A. Concetta's things yet? If by chance they are still to be sent, put in one of the girls' plates.3

6. Now let us come to you.4 Tell me: why do you make together all those silly resolutions, whispering in each other's ears, saying things that do your souls no good, being contrary to perfection and to your Rule?

7. It says: you shall be of one heart with your Superiors; you shall long for your Superiors to share fully in all your secrets, and you shall be glad every time you are corrected.5

8. Instead, here are your concerns and the whispering you have been doing these days: oh, we must be careful not to talk to the Mother, or rather watch how we talk, seeking every means to hide each of your actions from me and from Father, and many other things I have no time to put down now.

9. Tell me, our daughter, is it true?6 You see that this poor Mother of yours knows your affairs even from here.

10. Believe me, my blessed daughter, this way of behaving makes you lose all trust in your Superiors, who stand in the place of God.

11. Truly, I never gained so much trust in my Superior as when he reproved me and rebuked me for my faults.

12. With you it is quite the opposite: as soon as you are reproved and corrected, you lose trust at once and look for ways to hide from their eyes. Tell me, is it true?7

13. Come, stop puffing yourselves up with all your silly notions. Be simpler, and so you will always have the white feathers of the dove, and the black feathers of the crow will never grow on you.

14. Have pity on your soul, which you keep locked in the prison of your body. It weeps because it is in the house of its spouse and cannot enjoy him, nor even taste his delights, because you continually let it die, or rather languish for hunger of good works, of mortifications; the first are those of the tongue, and then those of the thoughts, driving them away, especially when they are against the Superiors; others are those of the palate, others those desires for worldly happiness that often cross your minds, others are to think little of your vocation and of the great grace God has given you.8 What do you think? Ah! Daughter, you who see so short a way, try to see far, and then your gaze will be on high and never on the low things of earth.9 Greet Sr. A. Vincenza for me; I will write to her soon; and for Carlotta I enclose a line here; pray much. Goodbye; the Lord bless you; I am your poor MOTHER ROSA

P.S. Maria is much better; today the Countess came to see me with Vincenza's note.10

Having been unable to speak to them before leaving, she warns them to be careful in speech. They should not make suppositions about a remark heard from the Superior, nor turn it into gossip. They should not go out walking, should love one another and pray.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Our daughters

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Being unable to say anything to you before I left about your fine way of acting and so many invented devilries, contrary as they are to your Rule and to what your Superiors have taught you.1

2. I cannot think what spirit has taken hold of you; I can only tell you that I would never have imagined that you, having misunderstood a remark of the Delegate Francesca, would use it as material for an ugly plot, confiding a thousand invented rumours to one another.2

3. Hellish tongue, better that you were always still than let loose in talk like this.3

4. I understand everything, and I do not intend this letter for all of you, only for those who know they have done what I wrote above.

5. Many times your Superiors have taught you how you should make your confession, and first of all they told you that to confessors you must tell your sins and, besides, whatever you need for your spirit, because your Rule commands this; all the more when we have confessors as upright and learned as Signor Defilippi,4 who by God's mercy truly guides us to perfection.

6. I will not dwell longer on this, because I want to touch briefly on another point. My God! It was never heard of that the poor Daughters of Saint Anne go out walking in threes! Horror! What ugly things, what thoughtlessness is this?5 Ah! How often the Holy Mother must have wept!

7. Try to make amends for the great harm done, and now that you are so few, love one another, and let charity accompany you in all your actions. Pray that God may send providence, and always believe me

Your affectionate MOTHER ROSA

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

1. Today I received your letter with the account; I very much regret having to tell you that you have spent more than all the other houses: you are 12 Religious, and in 6 months [you have spent more] than those here in Genoa, who are 15. They spent 1000 F. in a year, and you in six months. My God! What are those household expenses? When you had everything! Alas! How shall we carry on?

2. Ah! Squarzoni was unfortunately right when he complained to me.1 For pity's sake, consider that it will be a very serious matter for this poor Mother of yours. On every side I am pierced by thorns in every way.

9. For now I have nothing more to tell you, except, for charity's sake, to look after the schools, so that they go well and are satisfied; so they can truly see that they are being taught.8 God bless you. I want this letter to be taken as a daughter should hear a Mother's reproofs, and not as punishment and displeasure. I will say no more. I am ever your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA. Greet everyone for me; to you and all I wish the choicest blessings.

7. I am waiting for the papers from Merli, who never sends them, so everything drags on; I wish he would hurry and send them. Do me the kindness, if you can, of sending the money to the Superior at S. P. D'Arena, who really needs it; if you can — I cannot give it.

1. I could not write to you today as soon as the sisters arrived,1 because I was busy all day and Sr. A. Vincenza is at S. P. D'Arena. My dear, you cannot imagine how overwhelmed with work I am.

2. So the sisters arrived quite safely; I have read your letter and heard all that you are doing; everything is fine; and also that, while waiting, you are afraid I may turn up unexpectedly. Be of good heart; that does not even cross my mind.

3. Don't believe Secretary Parmigiani, because that is how he talks, but I know he can pay; he has the habit of complaining; don't give in; let him pay — make him pay, for he can. He always complains, and yet I know he has money.2

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

8. I commend to you the letter enclosed in this one;

for charity's sake, see that it reaches its destination safely. It would be good for you to act as sacristan, so as not to tire yourself so much, you and Sr.

1. A line, though late: it is nearly 2 after midnight. Today I received your letter about Sr. A. Carmelina. You can have her examined; her illness is already known, but it is good to call the doctor, and you can ask Monsignor which one to call.1

2. Another thing I have long wanted to write to you is that you should manage to see Ferri and tell him that it would be good to invite Countess Trotti to be president of his Congregation; do you understand me?2

3. Another thing. I would like you to send me at once 300 F. by money order or registered letter, asking at the post office which is safer, as I have a big deal to make. Pray that it goes well. Have them pray that I may soon conclude it, that is, close the contract, for then it will be a great benefit for the Daughters of Saint Anne; but the costs of the deeds require a lot of money.3 I am taking it from everywhere I know it is to be had.

affectionate MOTHER ROSA

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA. God bless you and all the others.

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I have just received your letter and cannot understand why you have not yet had Sr. A. Vincenza's letter telling you to send me the Rule at once — the version translated from the one in the church, which I must have left in the cupboard. If it isn't there, send me the Father's.1

2. For pity's sake, pack them securely; but I hope they are there and have the same cover as the first ones, you know, dark brown cardboard. You know; for charity's sake, look for them.

3. Send Maddalena away;2 the answer you gave Sr. A. Fortunata is right; I always reply like that to everyone. I do not want them meddling in anything without my permission.

4. I will write no more; take care, look after yourself, don't forget to take the pills, which will give you appetite and strength; it will all pass, but don't forget; in a word, look after yourself.

[Affectionate MOTHER ROSA]

She need no longer look for a house for her mother. Various advice about the Sisters. The Superior is coming from Sampierdarena; for charity's sake, she must not find out that the Father has been forbidden to come to the Mother House. A parcel will arrive from Sampierdarena; she should keep its contents; she will also receive various items for the house from Ferrara. Every day, new sorrows. She should have them pray. The letters she sent her are for the Father. He should answer at once.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. First of all, I let you know that Mamma no longer wants the house in Piacenza, because Emanuele has already left for Milan; so thank Don Gaetano and tell him that for now nothing more will be done, since the invalid has gone to another City.1

2. As for Sr. A. Maddalena, I forgot to write yesterday that you can perfectly well put her in the school, as you wrote; as for Sr. A. Elena, stand firm; let it be so. Have the doctor tell Sr. A. Zaveria that she needs to go to her native air, and then stand firm and tell her that when she is better she will come back. Meanwhile send for her relatives to come and fetch her.2 As for Father Agostino [and] Teresina, listen: the Superior of S. P. D'Arena is to come to accompany Giovanna.3

3. For charity's sake, let nothing leak out about that person who no longer comes. For charity's sake, let no one say anything, no one. You must keep an eye on her and arrange for her to leave soon.4 Give her Teresina, but only if the Marchioness wishes it. Let us not get into trouble.5

4. A parcel will reach you from S. P. D'Arena containing a velvet cloth, that is, a large piece of red velvet. I want it well kept, for charity's sake, and also a yellow chasuble and pieces of white satin. Keep everything carefully, especially the velvet and the chasuble.

5. From here you will receive an embroidery frame with two blouse fronts begun. Put them in the guest room, and also a bonnet with a pattern drawn on it; you can have this copied and then put it away too. You will see how lovely they are. Keep them carefully, and keep that place well shut, so that no dust gets into those rooms. You will also receive a large lamp; have it hung in the middle of the guest-room hall — I think there is a ring in the ceiling — and hang it on a cord. You will also find some very pretty stoppers for the little bottles in your refectory. For charity's sake, don't let them get dirty; they have had them here for ages, and if you saw how well they look! Also some nice plates for the girls, for when we have boarders. Keep these carefully too, and other little things I am sure will please you. I am trying to collect all I can, including a small chest of drawers,6 which we don't have; put it in the guest quarters, down there in the middle by the door where the chair is. You will see, and arrange everything as you think best.

6. Yesterday your letter did not surprise me at all about that kind person's curiosity, but you answered the truth very well. My dear, so many sorrows; every day new ones come.

7. What news have you of Volpe? Has Landi done nothing more about S. Lazzaro?7 Let us hope; today the month of May has begun; keep it fervently, so that Mary may be moved to pity for the Daughters of her Mother. Pray, for pity's sake.

8. If you think fit to send that surplice8 with its pattern to be embroidered or copied, you can send it with the pieces of white satin that will reach you from S. P. D'Arena.

9. Those letters you sent me were for the Father, because he must answer them. Immediately, yes; for charity's sake, get them to him at once and tell him to reply at once.

10. My God, tribulations on every side; here too there is a share. I really don't know where to turn for support [except] to the Heart of God, where I rest and leave you, calling myself ever yours, your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA. God bless you and all the others.

She should send the manuscript of the Constitutions already asked for. She will have a visit from the Princess. She is grateful to the Lord that the Princess did not come on the day she was in Piacenza. She should send her the surplice. Patience is needed: 1872 holds her in chains; 1873 will not be so. Courage and patience are needed. She is exhausted by the labours and worries of the house.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I am sending you the enclosed letter; send it on to its destination if he does not come. I am in the greatest distress because you have still not sent me the manuscript Constitutions I asked for.1 I fear the letter has gone astray — one, two, three letters, all lost then! For pity's sake send them to me at once.

2. I rejoice at the consolation you will have on Wednesday with the Princess visiting you. How good God is! Listen, daughter, this time he truly heard me, that she should not come on the day I was in Piacenza. I confess that for fear she might come I had the shakes for two days.2 I don't know why; it even pains me; on hearing her name every nerve in me shudders. For my part I can assure you that I pray for her and wish her a thousand blessings from Heaven, but what can I do!!!

3. Let us leave these useless things and come to the substance,

which for us is the house. Today I will write to the Bishop.3 I hear that Providence is coming; let us hope and always trust in God. Whoever trusts in Him alone will have everything. For the rest, you have done well in all you write me.

4. Yesterday I received a letter from Don Gaetano. He says nothing about Alessandro's slap. I hope you sent him the letter. He tells me he will come to settle Carolina's affairs.4 Well, do as you think; that way you will learn. Take heart and you will see that God will help you in everything.

5. You have not given me the surplice;5 if I had it I would have it begun. Listen, wrap it with a band crosswise, you know, the way the sheets of the receipt books are sent, that is, just one of the smaller ones, and send it to me here.

6. I hear what that person told you about Maddalena;6 well, do as he said. Show the house to the Parish Priest of Nizza too, and let it be in order.7 I hear about Sr. A. of the Good Shepherd; her turn will come too; let us be patient, for 1872 holds me in chains, but 1873 will not be so.

7. I hope so; everyone's turn comes; patience is needed; it is the Saints who beat the wicked; courage,8 if we want to win the victory. My dear, here too there are crosses without equal. I am drained of strength, for I can say that the wheel of this work always desfa(?) me blows and never rest; what anxiety.9

8. I hope you receive this tomorrow; that person will be there; I hope he will read this too, since I have no more time to add a line to his... from yesterday to today in this house — that is, as regards temporal affairs — I can tell you there are some very ugly things. My God! Pray, pray.

I am your poor

MOTHER ROSA

She answers a query, instructing her not to give a novice a dress or any other black clothing.1

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Two lines in haste, in reply to yours about Sr. A. Maddalena's things. I tell you she must not take away anything black2; if her parents sent it, that matters little; her parents had said they would give many other things that they never gave, so you see it comes to the same. I think we should be a little strict. If that person thinks fit, give this letter to the one who is going. Goodbye; I am your

poor MOTHER. I have received the Rule; all is well.3

She expresses satisfaction and approves all she has done. The lack of providence is felt in the Ferrara house too. She has been writing for hours; it is two in the morning. She will send the almost finished Constitutions to the Bishop next day. Once the debts are paid, she should see whether she can send her 100 francs. She should pray for the Delegate in Genoa, who is ill, and look after her own health.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Send this letter on to its destination at once. Today I received a long letter from you with much news of the house and the fine arrangements you have made. All is well.
