2. I hope you received the iron bed they sent you from Nizza; put it in Carlotta's room. I think the guest quarters will be fine now; nothing seems to be missing.

3. Listen, as for knocking down the infirmary, I would leave it as it is, because if some girl were to die, or there were others ill, you see, we wouldn't know what to do.1 Let us leave it as it is, and when the Lord sends providence we will arrange things differently.

4. My dear, here we are without providence; unless God works a miracle, it is a serious matter; my brain is wilting.2

5. Do you know what time I am writing? It will soon be two after midnight; I am alone in my room and, unable to sleep, I am writing — with spectacles now, because I can no longer see — having been sitting writing since 7 this evening; apart from the time for the rosary, I have written all the while.

6. In those Constitutions the works of piety are missing; I have had to supply everything from memory; I have now finished writing them; tomorrow I send them to His Eminence.3

7. Have them pray, for charity's sake, for I need it badly; here everything is going very badly. I hope to return soon to Piacenza; I have not yet written to the Bishop, but I will tomorrow.

8. As for the postulants, I would do this: tell the Parish Priest that both should enter together, and if one does not stay, the other's dowry should be bound to make it good, so that it doesn't happen that once they have placed with us the one with nothing, the other never comes;4 be very careful; take the names of all of them and of the Parish Priest, so that if we have to write we know to whom to address the letters.

9. You wrote to me about the flats Don Gaetano has found, but you don't tell me the prices; but do you know what I did? I had Sr. A. Vincenza write to Don Gaetano.5

10. When the Lord sends you enough to pay the miller, see whether you could send me about a hundred francs. Pay your debts first and then send them.

11. Late last night I received a letter [saying] that the Superior in Genoa was ill.6 I leave you to imagine what a blow this was for me; this morning I had another saying she was a little better; an inflammation of the throat, from one moment to the next.

12. Listen, think about taking care of yourself, for charity's sake, because you see how quickly it happens? Only this old dog of a mother of yours has bones like old dogs that never die.

13. As soon as I can I will write to the two wretched ones, Sr. A. En and Sr. A. Chi.7 Have them pray for this good Delegate, that she may soon be up again. They should take care that the girls who go to Church do not get up to tricks instead of praying, and should send one older and one younger girl together.8 Goodbye. I am your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA. God bless you all.

Some instructions. She should let her know when the trunk has arrived... She need not bother to send vegetables or other produce, as there is no need. She should approach the Prefect about the lottery.1

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. The Superior wrote to you about the sack; well, send only one; say nothing about the other, keep it.

2. I hope you can do everything I had written to you before the 13th of this month; that way things will be better.

3. Around the fifteenth (15th) the Superior of S. P. D'Arena will come and take Teresina with her, if the Marchioness wishes.2 When you have received the trunk, which should be today, write to me alone how you found everything and what was in it. I am sorry about the stoppers, there were no others. If it arrived safely, I will send you another with some plates for the girls. When there are services and other things (which) will be dear(?) to you. Hang the lamp now.3

4. Don't bother about vegetables, for they have everything here. Though if you have some in the garden, fine, but not much, for it would spoil; likewise only one salame, for charity's sake, because I repeat they have plenty here.

5. Send this on to its destination at once.4

6. Go and see the Prefect to commend the lottery to him and at the same time to see whether he has any good news for you about what he led us to hope for.5 You did well about Grandi; keep sending someone to see how his mother is.6 Tell the little girls I will write to them soon.7 Goodbye. I am your

Affectionate M. R. The Lord bless you

She has finished rearranging the Rule, which Mgr Giordani found "to his liking". It will be revised by Cardinal Vannicelli and sent by him to the S. Congregation. She will give him a detailed report in person.

Your Most Reverend Excellency,

1. Not having had the good fortune to come and receive Your Apostolic blessing while I was in Piacenza and to thank You warmly for all You do and have done for the poor Daughters of Saint Anne, whose gratitude will not fail, in prayers or in deeds, and wishing to give You the liveliest proofs of it, I now take up my pen to let You know that the reason was my poor health, as I was obliged to get up from my bed to resume the journey to Ferrara.1

2. Last night I finished rearranging the Rule; this morning I am expecting His Eminence's Secretary to hand it to him.2 Yesterday I had the honour of a visit from Monsignor Giordani, Bishop of Philadelphia, who looked over what I have written and, as far as I could tell, seemed to like it.3

3. It will soon be revised by His Eminence, who has undertaken, as he told me, to send it to the Sacred Congregation.4

4. Meanwhile I shall return to Your Feet and give You a full and detailed report in person.

5. Grant me Your Apostolic blessing, which I humbly await, as I declare myself Your Most Reverend Excellency's

most humble Servant Sr. A. MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

She has handed the manuscript of the Constitutions to Cardinal Vannicelli for revision and comments. She wishes to know whether the copy to be sent to the S. Congregation of Bishops and Regulars must be printed.

Your Most Reverend Excellency,

1. Forgive me if I trouble You again with my tiresome handwriting, availing myself of the permission Your Excellency gave me when I was there, allowing me to write to You whenever I needed.

2. Today I handed the manuscript of the Constitutions to His Eminence for him to make the necessary observations;1 I should like to know whether, to be submitted to the Sacred Congregation, it must be printed.

3. His Eminence will send it to Your Excellency himself, and I shall wait with the keenest desire for the longed-for moment of the Decree of Praise; then, as I told You once before, I shall have the good fortune to be at Your Feet to tell You all that weighs on my soul.

4. My health goes from bad to worse, and every day I see the blessed moment of my departure drawing nearer, always hoping first to leave the Lord's Work firmly established.2

5. Deign to bless me, and may Your blessing bring me the strength I so much need. Deign to accept my humble respects as I remain Your Most Reverend Excellency's most humble Sr. A. MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

She recalls an earlier request for a subsidy for the girls in their care and renews it, trusting in his kindness.

Your Excellency,

1. The Superior, whom I sent in my place to ask Your Excellency whether through You the Government had yet granted what You have so kindly pursued for our poor little girls, who are in extreme need, not having had the good fortune to find You at the Palace, I take the liberty of reminding You of the matter in writing, though I am sure Your noble heart has not forgotten it.

2. The need in which this house finds itself urges me to beg You earnestly, sure of finding in You a kind father1 who will not delay in taking it up, so that this house may soon be helped in its many needs.

3. If my request were not too bold, I would ask You for a line bringing me some comforting news amid the many adversities in which I find myself. Please accept, Your Excellency, my respects, as with the deepest esteem and respect I sign myself Your Excellency's most humble Sr. ANNA M. G. R.

She hopes the Vernengo sisters and Don Luigi have received her letters. She urges observance of the timetable, otherwise there will be backsliding and providence will fail. She greets all the sisters and Don Luigi.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I did not answer your letter at once because my occupations are too many to discharge them punctually. I hope the Vernengo sisters1 have received my letters, and Don Luigi too.2 Yesterday I received two lines from him, enclosing one addressed to me.

2. I urge you to have the timetable kept exactly, from rising in the morning to retiring at night. If this is done, the Lord's blessing will not be lacking in that house; otherwise everything will go back to swaddling clothes3 and God will withhold His divine Providence.

3. How is Sr. A. Angiola? Let us hope we can replace her soon;4 I hear that in Genoa (?).5

4. Yesterday I received letters from the Vernengo sisters; I enclose one here for the sick girl.6 I will say no more because my health is poor. Greet all the Sisters and Don Luigi for me, and believe me your very poor

MOTHER S. A. M. ROSA 465

She encloses a letter for the Father. From him she will learn whether she should send a letter of hers. If she receives money, she should pay the debts.1

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. In haste I send you these two lines to tell you to send this on at once. I will write to you at greater length.

2. You will hear from the person what I am telling him. Should I send it?2

3. If money comes to you, keep it and try to pay where you can. We have some here.3 I am yours.

Goodbye.

As for Saveria, I was saying to send her home for a change of air.4 I am your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

She should send the finished paintings to Countess Caracciolo. When she arrived in Piacenza the Countess kindly visited her and brought her the sum of money she needed. Her worries are countless. Her only relief, so as not to faint, is recourse to the Crucifix, putting her lips to the "divine fountains" of the most holy blood.

A.M.F.

My good Father Agostino,

1. I have received your letter telling me the paintings are finished and asking where to send them.1 I would like them all to go to Piacenza, but I was afraid that the one of the Holy Mother in which the painter will have included the Eternal Father2 might be taken from me and the other given me instead; I would be very sorry. But if you, Father Agostino, are sure this will not happen, then send them all together to Piacenza, to Countess Caracciolo.

2. You ask about this good Lady.3 I can tell you that as soon as I reached Piacenza I sent word to her, knowing she wanted to speak to me, and as I was too ill to go, she had to come to me, and she brought me the interest on the house, which falls due these days.4 I blessed God for it and this good Countess, praying that the Lord may fill her with the graces she desires.

3. What a weight she took off my mind! Believe me, good Father, my worries are immense and my little head can no longer bear them. You know well that nothing is given us here any more; so this poor house too is full of tribulations and left to Providence, where we thought there was support.5 My God!

4. Let us rejoice at the thought that our Eternal Father deigns to press his divine hand upon this unworthy servant of his... I bless him, and laying everything at his feet, most tranquil on the cross where I find myself, I rest happily.6

5. When I feel myself fainting, I put my lips to one of the divine fountains of my Crucified One to take a sip of refreshment. Having drunk of that Most Holy Blood, I need nothing more; glad and strong I return to my work, which I am so poor at perfecting; indeed, in all truth I find that I always spoil it.7

6. The prayers you wanted are being said, but of course, as mine are among them, everything goes wrong, as one sees happening in other things. Meanwhile I thank you infinitely for all you do and have always done for this poor work.

7. The Rule is finished and I have already handed it to His Eminence.8 Now let God act. I can assure you that man had no part in it, and so I hope that, if not this time then another, it will be crowned with approval. God grant that this unworthy servant of his may see it, for I am galloping towards the end, or at least towards an illness.9

8. How I suffer, my God! You alone know it!! Paradise, you are so far away that truly great efforts are needed to reach you, since one cannot go up by carriage. And you know that I cannot go on foot because of my weakness; so all that remains is toil, and it takes me long, and then I always find big stones, which are my infirmities, and when I stumble on them I have to stop and find strength, ways to appease divine justice, and ask it to help me tread them down.10

9. I find I have no more paper, so I must stop; so it will be at the end of my days: I shall still have so much to put right in my poor soul and no more time; I grow ever more wretched. Believe me yours in Jesus

most humble and obliged Sr. ANNA MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

She gives instructions about some girls and a Sister. She wants to go to Piacenza, at least for a few days. She has asked the Prefect for a subsidy; the Superior should ask Councillor Grandi. The thought of how little help comes from benefactors tears her soul.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I have your letter and reply at once; as for the Carnevali girl, you did well; stand firm, let them put her in hospital; in short, let them take her away as soon as possible; and try to get the Ferrari girl to go too.1 You tell me about Teresina: go yourself to the Marchioness Anguissola and say: "Marchioness, I have come to hear what you wish for your Teresina, because for her every exception will be made, and you know well that whatever you wish will be done". Then do as she tells you.2

2. As for Sr. A. Maddalena, let her ask pardon for a week and tell the Sisters to pray to the Holy Mother for her that she may amend. Then hear what that person says.3

3. I hear what you tell me about that woman; you answered her well; it is the pious busybodies who need to have the confessor tied to their skirts; all confessionals are a show to me; even a church door is a confessional for me.4

4. Daughter, sincerity, charity, the love of God — that is all we need; everything else is a fine nothing, and less than nothing.5

5. I hope you received Sr. A. Vincenza's letter. My dear, I would be glad if I had to leave and come to you, because here I have no room, truly camping out; I assure you it is real suffering for me. So pray and have them pray that I may be called somewhere;6 then on the way I will stop with you for a few days.

6. I no longer know where my head is, it is so upside down; I have had someone write to the Prefect about the money;7 you see to pestering Grandi, so that we can start repairing the wall and paying out the few pennies they mentioned.8 What a worry this matter of providence is! It robs me of rest, it tears my soul. Patience! My God, what sorrows these are. Goodbye for now. God bless you. The Superior in Genoa is better.9 I am yours, in haste, your poor

MOTHER ROSA

She has learned from the Superior of the Piacenza House of the dire financial situation caused by heavy debts. Knowing her motherly kindness, she turns to her, sure of her providential help for the many little girls, who will be the precious gems of her crown before God's throne.

Most Illustrious Marchioness,

1. This poor creature of yours comes to you most sorrowful and filled with the most painful affliction, having nowhere to lean except on her whom she found a compassionate Mother to her poor daughters of this most desperate1 House of the Daughters of Saint Anne in Piacenza.

2. The state in which the Superior writes that this wretched House finds itself wrings my heart with grief: 1400 F. owed to the miller, 600 F. to the baker, another 300 for pasta, and more I will not list so as not to weary you.2 Ah! for pity's sake, be moved to compassion and help them. They have no other support but you.

3. Marchioness, one day these little girls will be, before God's throne, so many precious gems around your crown. In my misery I raise prayers for you to God every day, wretched though they are; I trust in His mercy that He will accept them and grant all your desires.3 Knowing how great is the generosity of your heart, I dare to hope you will not leave unanswered this plea of your most humble Sr. A. M. R.

She is very anxious, fearing that letters addressed to the Father have gone astray. She has sent four. If they arrived, they should let her know by telegram; if not, make enquiries and complaints at the post office. It happens that letters do not arrive and then news contained in them is repeated by others. A visitor and a postulant will arrive. She will soon send her two trunks.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. My daughter, today your letter worried me greatly, because you did not tell me you had received another of mine meant for that person, with a few lines inside for you. Alas! Can it have gone astray? It was dated the 2nd of this month. That person should have received 4: one of the 30th, another of the 2nd, another of the 3rd, one of the 4th.1

2. For pity's sake, relieve me of this anxiety. If these letters arrived, send him these two lines at once together with this letter of yours for him to read.2 I am extremely agitated; indeed, if you have received them all, let me know by telegram, saying: "We have received them all".

3. If by chance they have gone astray,3 make enquiries and shout at the post office staff and the director too, telling him we are tired of this post office where letters are always lost and then we find things being repeated to us here and there. What a way to behave! Speak to Merli about it and tell him the Mother is very displeased, as indeed she is.4

4. I was telling you about the Parish Priest; I said you should carry on and handle the matter yourself, which is right; tell him I wrote that I cannot deal with these things and that we should leave the Superior to do what she thinks best for her house, and give him many compliments from me.5

5. She did well to write, or rather telegraph, to the Superior that Giovanna's uncle and aunt are coming to fetch her; but there is Giustina. Well, if she comes, receive her well and make a great fuss of her.6

6. Listen, the Superior in Genoa writes that in a few days that widowed Lady is coming, perhaps at the end of the week. I hope you have done all I wrote and will do everything quickly, won't you? Then she will find everything in order; but I would put her in the refectory.7

7. I leave you to see where it will be best, as there are only two postulants in the small refectory I told you to set up; with the door open the reading can be heard.

8. I have arranged for another postulant, who will bring almost a thousand francs; of course if you tell that person that in the letter dated the 2nd — two — I spoke to him about the girls he asked me about. My God! I don't know what to think; I was telling him something very important.

9. Write to me at once; relieve me of this anxiety. I will no longer write so plainly, not even to you, because it was a letter in which I told you many things, including matters of business.

10. Today I wrote to the Marchioness.8 I hope she will send something. Let us pray. In a few days I will send you another trunk; I hope you will be pleased.

As it is no use here, you can make use of it; perhaps there will be two: one of Maddalena's and the other of Antonia's, then you understand.9 For certain matters I will have the Superior write to you. (I am yours).

How is Sr. A. Eufemia?10 Greet everyone for me, and receive a thousand good wishes from one who calls herself ever your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

She is not really convinced by what the Superior tells her. If she had received all the letters, she would have sent what was asked. She has written to Don Gaetano to apologize; the Superior should do the same. She cannot complain about the correspondence: if she checks it she will find that never two days passed without a letter from her.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Yesterday I received a letter from you assuring me that you had received all my letters. I tell you that if you had received my letters you would have sent me what I was asking for and so insistently told both you and that person to send; so, if you have not done it, it is a sign that neither of you received the letters, otherwise you would have mentioned it.1

2. Now to the matter of Don Gaetano. He wrote to me and I answered at once asking his pardon, and you will do the same.2 This is the penance I impose on you; so we have done it together, and since I did it first, it will be easier for you to do your part.

3. Today Sr. A. Vincenza is sending you the trunk and a small chest of drawers.

4. You mention whitewashing the little rooms; it seems unnecessary to me, but if you see the need, do as you think.3

5. You ask whether you did wrong to break it off. You did right, but you should have acted differently. What an ugly word anger is! I really cannot bear to hear it; it pains me greatly. It offends the heart of the Holy Mother.4

6. Yesterday you will have received another. Now I close because I have many things to do; but don't think badly, for in truth you are too demanding; when you look over the letters I wrote you, I think you will find that two days never passed.5

God bless you; believe me always your

Affectionate M. ROSA GATTORNO

Regarding the girl he recommended, it had been agreed that whenever she showed signs of illness he would take her back. Now her condition is such that she cannot keep her, having other children. They should try to send her to the baths, and once cured she may return.

Very Reverend Parish Priest,

1. Forgive me for not replying at once to your esteemed letter, which I had the pleasure of receiving, owing to my many occupations.

2. Thank you for the prayers you offer; I am most obliged to you for them.

3. As for your protégée, Your Reverence knows the agreement we made, that whenever she showed signs of illness they would take her back immediately; now I tell you that I absolutely cannot keep her, for my conscience forbids it, since we have other children entrusted to us.1

4. Meanwhile let them try to send her to the baths, where she can be admitted for 60 F., and in the meantime she may recover.

5. On her return, once improvement is certain, she may come back in; otherwise she will go from bad to worse, and I am instructing the Superior to have her taken to her parents.

6. This is all I have decided to do, as I cannot do otherwise.

7. Your Reverence knows how much it pains me to use such language, though I am sure that, if I did not do this, Your Reverence would advise me to.

Please accept my most distinguished greetings, a remembrance of

me before your Crucifix, and believe me, as I remain with all esteem and respect Your Reverence's most humble and obliged Servant [Sr. A. M. ROSA GATTORNO]2

The Piacenza house, as the Superior writes, is in extreme want. She turns to her, confident that, as on other occasions, she will be heard. She thanks and greets her.

Most Illustrious Marchioness,

1. The poor House in Piacenza, the Superior writes, is in great want; you know that our Angel has been taken from us, good Marchioness; so, for charity's sake, please do not forget it, especially now that all my little girls are short of clothing.1

2. I well remember that whenever I turned to you in my needs, your charity never left my request unanswered, so this thought comforts me that in this too I shall be heard.

3. I assure you that in our feeble prayers Your Ladyship and your whole excellent family are always remembered as our benefactress, as you have always been, and our glorious Mother Saint Anne will surely deign to hear us by filling you with heavenly blessings.

Please accept, Most Illustrious Marchioness, my most distinguished and respectful greetings; share them with your most worthy daughters, and believe me with all esteem and respect Your Ladyship's

most humble Sr. ANNA M. R. G.

She is still in Ferrara, as the revision of the Rule is not finished. She asks whether her presence in Rome will be needed once the Rule has been sent to the S. Congregation. She has written to Mgr Vitelleschi; she asks whether the Rule should be submitted printed or in manuscript. He should plead her cause with Fr Angelini. She hopes to take on another hospital. Her health is as usual.

A.M.F.

My good Father Agostino,

1. I have received your letter and, having a scrap of time, I use it to reply. As you see from the date, I am still in Ferrara, because the Rule has not yet been revised.1

2. Father Agostino, I would like one thing: that at your convenience you find out whether, when His Eminence has sent it to Rome, it would be good for me to come, or whether this most eminent Prelate's recommendation will suffice.2

3. I have also written to Bishop Vitelleschi to ask whether I should have it printed before sending it to the Sacred Congregation, and I should like to know whether he received my letter and what he instructs:3 whether I must have it printed or His Eminence should send it as it is. In any case it will be sent by the Cardinal.

4. You might mention it to Father Angelini.4 Ask him why he never answers my letters; I have already sent him two and he never replies; true, I am not worthy of it. Tell him, Father Agostino; I don't know how to thank you, but God will reward you, and this wretched creature will not cease to remember it every day — as she does — before the throne of the Most High; but my prayers are very wretched; you have had proof of that.

5. I tell you nothing from here, because I can say nothing certain. Now everything is in the hands of Father Angelini, who has taken Father Manfredini's place.5 Father Agostino, for pity's sake, earnestly commend to this good religious the poor work of God, which so much needs it.

6. I hope soon to take on another Hospital near Piacenza,6 where they make good wine; so when we are there, I hope good Father Agostino will come and drink a glass. Oh! how much better would be the sweet wine from Jesus' cellar; I like that too, and I would need it badly to gain a little strength, which I always lack and which diminishes every day.

7. I won't speak of my health, which is always the same. Weakness is taking my sight, and I can no longer write or read without spectacles. Father Agostino, we are old, and so everything ends; our deeds are all that remain.

8. Forgive the poor handwriting. I hope soon to receive a letter from you telling me something about what I ask.

9. If you see Vitelleschi, kiss his ring for me, with a blessing that I so much desire.

Meanwhile send me your blessing and believe me always your very poor

Sr. ANNA M. ROSA GATTORNO

She should not distress herself over what was said: the lost letter was not her fault, nor need she send anything. Some directions for the house. The Marchioness has sent a gift. She had hoped for more substantial help. Prayer will obtain providence; Mary will help the poor Daughters of her Mother, and the large rooms of the house can be arranged more practically.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Yesterday I received your letter, which pained me because you ask my forgiveness, when the loss of the letter is the post office's fault, not yours. What have you to do with it? Strange girl! And besides you fret about asking what you should send me. More real nonsense: I no longer need what you were to send me, and if I did I would have repeated what I said in the letter that went astray.1 Your anxieties have no purpose, because they are all products of imagination. Put them all in a corner; they are worth nothing.2

2. Let us come to practical matters:

1st - Send Elena home at once, at once.3

2nd - About the sack, I already told you to wait until you have plenty in the garden, because they have everything here.4

3. I am very sorry to hear of poor Delfina's bad state. I approve of your sending Sr. A. Cherubina to the house at the Morte and withdrawing Sr. A. Eufemia.5 I hear of the Marchioness's 200 F. I had written to her that you needed, as is true, 3000 F.; it seems impossible; the very stones would have been moved by what I said in that letter.6

4. So you have done everything for the house. You mention the cruets for the guest quarters. I will send them, and something else too.

5. Let us pray the Lord to send a little providence, so that we can have work done in those ugly large rooms where the girls used to be.7 Then everything will be in order in this very poor house.

6. I hope dear Mary will help the poor Daughters of her Mother, especially in this month; if you pray, it will come; if it doesn't come, it is a sign that the prayers are said without fervour. I pray a great deal, but my prayers are worth nothing.

7. Goodbye, because I was called and left the [...].8 I don't know when I can come, because too many things keep me here.

Goodbye again. Believe me your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA. God bless you all

8. P.S. Whom have you put as cook at the Morte? The names you are to give the postulants: Sr. A. M. Battistina, Sr. A. Giovannina.9 Send this letter on to its destination at once.10

She sends her suitable material for the parlour curtains. Plumbing material sent from Sampierdarena will be delivered to her; she should keep it. She has decided on a postulant's Clothing but wants to know from the Father how to proceed. She urges her to imitate the Holy Mother in the virtues a Superior needs: gentleness above all; courage, patience, resignation to God's will; and trustful recourse to Jesus in prayer.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My blessed daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. This morning I received your letter telling me that good Ferrari has died.1 God the Father's will be done!2 Then you said you still need material for the curtains, because one window is uneven; I am sending you at once about 20 metres of material for the parlour window curtain. You will see it is very suitable; make it nice and large. I am also sending the cruets, which I hope will arrive unbroken.

2. You will receive from S. P. D'Arena 16 metres of lead water pipe; keep it. Soon more will reach you from Genoa, together with sheets of lead or zinc and a pump. Keep everything.2

3. The Sisters at S. P. D'Arena tell me that they sent you all the pieces of satin. Check; there were some large ones. Keep these to make a conopeum for Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate, since the one for solemn feasts is old; tell me how many stoppers are missing and I will try to buy them for you.

4. I want to know from that person what I should do on Sunday when clothing Antonietta. I thought it best to do everything myself; I won't write why, because the fear that it may be lost like the letter of the 2nd makes me feel truly... Patience.3

5. You always write to me sad and full of resentment; I tell you that all your anxieties are based on falsehood.4 Now it is all past; I urge you to gentleness, for this is the true character of a Daughter of Saint Anne, M.4 of the Immaculate. If we are to imitate the Mother, this is what we must do;5 otherwise we shall never be recognized as daughters of so Holy a Mother and shall remain among the reprobate.6

6. Come, courage, patience, resignation to God's will; with this we shall give good example.

7. Superiors are the shadow of the other religious, who all run after them and go where the shadow shows them the way. Do you see a mother who is irritable, always shouting, always with a sad face? Then all the children do the same, and order no longer reigns [in] that family: some shout on one side, some scream on the other; in the end the devil sleeps on their roofs, having no more work to do, because little by little they end up gravely offending the Lord.

8. Patience, docility and resignation are the qualities God requires a good Superior to have.

9. Are you upset? Run to the Church and cry out with Jesus, weep, and then, once you have dried your tears, back to work, all things to all and full of sweet unction to pass on to others. Goodbye; I am your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

10. We have received the receipt book and the pyx veil.5 If you have those small pieces of white silk, send them to me. God bless you all, and you in particular. Send [this] letter of mine on to its destination at once.6

She writes to spare her anxiety. She should send the sisters to Nizza, as Sr. A. Vincenza told her. Plenty of postulants will come to her later. She gives news of Carlotta.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

[Good Superior, ...]1

1. Having a little strength and a little time, I am writing to you myself, to show you that I am on my feet [and] you need not worry.

2. Listen to what Sr. A. Vincenza tells you: send to Nizza a clothed postulant who is not from Nizza2 and Sr. A. Ernesta, on Monday without fail, because they don't know what to do and are in extreme need.3

3. As for you, postulants will come to you, even more than you want. I have written to that person to send you some. Have you accepted both? Then there are already two.4

4. Goodbye; I am yours. We shall see each other soon. For charity's sake, send the sisters to Nizza at once. And in the sisters' trunk, or sack, however you send it, please put Carlotta's dress, the percale one that should be in the wardrobe. Send the letter.

5. Goodbye. Cepinetto is having a grand ball; I hope the floor he dances on gives way soon and he breaks his head. Carlotta, the little temptation, shouts "anger!" and drives everyone to despair; she works and embroiders a great deal; she has made two lovely caps, one for Signor Grandi and the other for Merli.5

[your most affectionate MOTHER ROSA]

Her Daughters of the Nizza community are overjoyed at the Pastor's kindness and goodwill towards them. She thanks him and asks for his letter of "commendation", to be sent with those of the Bishops of the other dioceses where the Daughters of Saint Anne work, to the S. Congregation in support of the recently revised Constitutions.

Your Most Reverend Excellency,

1. The welcome Your Excellency deigned to give me when I first had the privilege of coming to receive Your blessing left me with the liveliest sense of Your great kindness, and today it was confirmed by a most consoling letter from my Religious in Nizza, telling me, full of joy, how great Your Most Reverend Excellency's Charity towards them was. This obliges me to express in writing what I regretfully could not say in person, as it would have been a great consolation to me to be in that poor Hospital in Nizza on the day Your Most Reverend Excellency honoured them with Your blessing.

2. But the affairs of the Institute keep me in Ferrara, the Sacred Congregation having entrusted to His Eminence Cardinal Vannicelli the revision of our Constitutions; so I hope, with God's help, that in a few days they will be sent to Rome.1

3. On this occasion, needing letters of commendation from all the Ordinaries of the dioceses where our poor Houses are, I am collecting them, and I now come to Your feet begging You to kindly send Yours as well, in the hope that You will put in it a word no less than all the others.

4. My gratitude, and that of the Institute, will never diminish towards You, whether in obedience or on any occasion that arises for us to show You our thanks.

5. Deign to send me Your Apostolic blessing, which I humbly await, declaring myself with the greatest veneration Your Most Reverend Excellency's most humble Sr. A. MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

Since she cannot sleep, she spends time with her. It is the vigil of Pentecost. May God fill them with the fire of his Spirit and his light so that they may guide their Communities well, forming them in the spirit of the Rule and in love for Saint Anne, and be an example in the practice of silence. Jesus dwells where silence dwells. The little girls have written to her; she is glad they pray for her. As for the house, she suggests moving some beds and some building work to make the rooms more practical. She should first call the master builder to check the cost, for money is needed, in the other houses too, and there is none.1

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

My daughter,

1. Today you will have received a letter written in three hands. Since I cannot sleep tonight, I will spend some time with you. First of all let us talk a little about God and about tomorrow's beautiful day, the day of the Holy Spirit.2

2. Ah! would that God might fill your hearts with this fire and furnish your minds with heavenly lights, so that you may direct your Communities well,3 instil in them the true spirit of the Holy Rule, love for Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate, their Mother and teacher, and by example lead them to practise holy silence, for without it one cannot have a holy and good community; there can be no peace, only scheming and constant quarrels. For pity's sake, where there is much noise, only the devil reigns.

3. Jesus is where silence dwells; it is then that he lives there and speaks to hearts, rekindles them, enlightens them; but whoever is always going about with a wagging tongue, like me, will surely never receive anything, and their salvation will always be in doubt.4

4. Peace, peace, silence, calm, and then you will feel God coming to speak to your heart with words all sweet and loving.5

5. The little girls wrote to me, but I have no time to reply; tell them their letters are very dear to me, because they always tell me they are praying hard for me; but for charity's sake let them keep on fervently, because I have not yet obtained anything; indeed, there is not even hope of obtaining it.

6. I do not want to suspect that their prayers are badly said or lacking fervour; rather I attribute everything to my wickedness and all my infamies, which hold back the graces.

7. God bless you, my dears, and believe that, although this poor Mother of yours is far away, her thoughts are on you, for your temporal and spiritual welfare. Goodbye.6

8. Now to the Religious; that means the refectory will now be empty; you have only 23 Religious left. I hear Eufemia sleeps [...].7 It would be good to put her in the little room called the clock room; you can have the harmonium taken out and put in the guest quarters, the chairs in your room, and put a bed for her there. It is a pity for her to soil those beds you have arranged in your room.

9. Now I would like you to make up her bed in Carlotta's room, and Sr. A. Vincenza's too; I remember that you sleep there,8 but then you can sleep in your own room. If a little providence had come, I would have liked you to have the clock room divided with a brick partition and its own door, to make a room for the Superior.9

10. And so Sr. A. Eufemia could for the moment be put in the room called the shoe room; indeed, put her there right away, and anyone needing to go to the little closet can go through the door near St Joseph.

11. I would also have liked that little closet which, you know, is in the large courtyard10 to have that door closed and a small door opened on the side of the girls' kitchen; then the girls would not have to cross the courtyard, that is, go down the well staircase, but use the small one leading to the little room where they keep the sewing. They would go to this privy and it would be much more convenient.

12. But if providence doesn't come, what can we do? I don't know where to turn, so full is my head with the worry that, as you will have read, Sforza wants to be paid, and it is not 1000 F. but a full 30,000 L.; what a thing! Who would have said I should be reduced to such tremendous humiliations!11 If only God would accept them!

13. I would gladly make a trip there, but incognito, without anyone knowing; on the other hand, to come for a day and then leave — I hardly know myself.

14. What do you think of my idea about the privy? You see, it would stop the girls wandering about. You know, so often a priest comes down, and there is a girl alone coming to the cellar,12 and then the little ones, always with the fear that they may linger by the well; instead the door of the last refectory, where Giovanna used to be, would be used, and the girls could no longer come out.13

15. I would think it would not cost much. You should call the master builder and hear what he says. What can I say? I am downcast, because there are great expenses everywhere and no one ever comes who really does something for the Institute. Patience!

16. Have them pray for providence, which we truly need. Meanwhile at S. Lazzaro they have still done nothing, nor for the house at the Morte.14

17. As for Grandi, it would be good for you to pay him a visit; but do as you think, for I don't know the local customs.15

18. When you read this letter, I want you to study it carefully, so that you will not make me repeat things as I see you do. For charity's sake, I have so little time, and then it pains me. Goodbye.

[Your affectionate MOTHER ROSA]

19. The numbers of the cups you are to send to S. P. D'Arena will be Nos. 91, 92, 93; do you understand? So there are four: 91, 92,

93, 94. I will tell you why in person.16

She has blessed the Lord for the new Daughters of Saint Anne and prayed for them. But at the same time she has been wounded by disobedience to a precise instruction of hers. The Superior should ask God's pardon for the fault.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Today I had news of your ceremony, of the new Daughters of Saint Anne and how lovely it was; I blessed God for it and held the new brides close in His heart, asking Him to communicate to them the true spirit of our Holy Rule, so that they may become beloved daughters of Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate;1 but I could not enjoy it without a cruel wound on hearing that so little heed was paid to my words and that obedience at that moment no longer counted.2

2. My God! How your heart must have been wounded when no heed was paid to what you wished! I had instructed the Superior of Genoa to take her two postulants back to Genoa after the ceremony, because I thought it best. She obeyed, showing her what I had written. And no attention was paid to this; on the contrary, they insisted that she too should stay and, having seen they could not persuade the Superior, kept back one sister, Sr. A. Eletta; something that would have displeased me greatly.3

3. I want to take it as an oversight, perhaps a failure to think about what the Superior said; otherwise the fault would be too serious. In any case, ask God's pardon for it, and the Holy Mother's. I add no more because it is late.

4. Greet Sr. A. Giuseppa of Jesus for me, and her sister.4 In due course I will answer her letters; for now I cannot. I am telling her nothing, because I have put everything in Don Accinelli's hands.5 I am too busy and have no time to think of anything else. For two days I have had a bad headache; the desk wears out my brain.

Goodbye; the Lord bless you; believe me

your affectionate MOTHER ROSA

5. My respects to Don Luigi; tell him I would like to know something about the hospital; what does he say? Shall we win or be put to flight?6

She has been told of his improper interference in the Boys' School, which is under her personal direction. She hopes the reports are unfounded; otherwise she would be compelled, against her will, to take the appropriate measures.

Very Reverend Parish Priest,

1. I am informed, as a certainty, that you intend to put lay teachers in the Morte Schools; I find it hard to believe; in any case, I warn you that, since the Schools are under my jurisdiction and direction, I do not want any teacher paid by you or by the public there.1

2. I am also told that, without my knowledge, Your Reverence has sent a petition to the Town Council for subsidies, declaring the Schools to be yours and under your direction.2

3. I would like to believe that there is no truth in the rumours I have frankly set out to you here; otherwise I would be compelled to take a decision that would be very unpleasant to me and hardly satisfactory to Your Reverence, to whom I remain with all respect Your Reverence's most humble Sr. ANNA M. R. G.

The Superior at Sampierdarena has told her of the favourable inclination to employ the Daughters of Saint Anne in the new Hospital. She thanks him, hoping to express her gratitude in person.1

Most Illustrious Sir,

1. I have heard from the Superior of the Sampierdarena House that the Honourable Town Council, through Your Lordship, would be willing to employ the Daughters of Saint Anne to nurse the sick in the new Hospital.2 I thank Your Lordship infinitely for thinking of us.

2. You will always find us willing and ready at your call. Besides offering you our service, I thank you infinitely for the preference shown us, and I wish an occasion would arise to show you my gratitude better than in words; I hope you will soon confirm it with a reply.

Please accept, Most Illustrious Sir, my most distinguished greetings, and kindly convey them to your Most Illustrious Wife; believe me Your Lordship's most humble Sr. A. M. ROSA GATTORNO

She thanks him for his letter and the "letter of commendation", which she has already handed to Cardinal Vannicelli.

Your Most Reverend Excellency,

1. I could not at once thank Your Most Reverend Excellency for Your most esteemed letter and for the letter of commendation You kindly sent me, as I was away from Ferrara.1 As soon as I returned I hastened to fulfil so great a duty, expressing as best I can the keen gratitude my soul feels for the great favour You deigned to do me.2 I have already handed it to His Eminence Cardinal Vannicelli, who was much pleased with it.

2. Most Reverend Excellency, wretched as I am, I dare assure You that in my helplessness I turn to God together with the whole community, begging Him to fill You with every grace that can be desired.

Deign to bless me, as I await it prostrate at Your feet, remaining with the greatest veneration Your Most Reverend Excellency's most humble Sr. A. MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

She asks the Town Council to bear the cost of sea-bathing treatment for two girls placed in the Institute by the Council itself.

Most Illustrious Councillor,

1. As we have in our poor house two girls placed by the Honourable Town Council who need sea-bathing, and we cannot bear the necessary expense, I beg Your Lordship to take on this charge, so as to provide1 for the health of these poor creatures.2

2. Confident that you will take it up, I thank you in advance and sign myself with the greatest esteem and respect Your Lordship's

most humble Sr. ANNA M. R. G.

The Superior in Genoa has often written to her of his charitable interest in the House. She not only implores heaven's blessings on him but feels bound to express her warmest gratitude. May he always count the Daughters of Saint Anne among his poor.

Most Illustrious Sir,

1. Very often I find your charitable name written in the letters of the Superior in Genoa, telling me of the great charity Your Lordship shows this poor House.

2. I therefore address my feeble prayers to the Most Holy Virgin, begging her to pour out her choicest blessings on you; but a just duty obliges me to tell Your Lordship of the keenest gratitude this most wretched Servant of the Lord feels towards you, assuring you that every day the Community offers prayers to the Most High for the welfare of so great a benefactor.

3. I was recently sent from Rome a great many booklets and prayers of St Aloysius; I venture to send you some, knowing how well Your Lordship can make use of them for the Glory of this dear Saint.1

4. Please accept, Most Illustrious Sir, my warmest thanks, with the request that you continue your kindness to the poor Daughters of Saint Anne, counting them among your poor, who so much need help.2

With the most distinguished esteem and respect, Your Lordship's most humble Sr. A. M. ROSA GATTORNO

She is grateful for his kind welcome in Genoa and his interest in the new House opened there. She thanks him and asks him to continue his kindness to the Sisters. The Superior of the House has been kindly received by the Bishop, which gives her consolation and hope. She would like to know his opinion, if possible in writing, of the Religious' charitable work.

Very Reverend Secretary,

1. My poor health and constant occupations are the only reason I could not fulfil sooner a wish and duty I owe Your Reverence, namely to tell you that I have kept the memory of the welcome and kindness you showed me when I had the privilege of meeting you in Genoa, and that the interest you showed in the poor new House there, of the poor Daughters of Saint Anne, left me with the liveliest gratitude towards Your Reverence.1 I hope in your great kindness you will excuse my long delay in thanking you, forgive me, and continue your kindness and protection to the poor Daughters of Saint Anne.

2. The Superior of the House there2 visited His Excellency Monsignor Magnasco last week, and he kindly received her graciously; this was no small consolation to me.

3. I hope to receive your blessing when I come to Genoa, and meanwhile, if it were not too bold, I would ask for a line from you assuring me that the Charity of those poor Religious is always in accordance with their wishes.3

4. How glad I would be if, in sending me your blessing, you would kindly give me some word of it; I would be most grateful.

5. I also ask you to obtain for me His Excellency's blessing, as with heartfelt esteem and veneration I sign myself Your Reverence's most humble Sr. A. MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

The priest Angelo Ricchini has again gone to court, and she, unable to go to Genoa because she is engaged in Ferrara in completing the Rule, has appointed Don Antonio Accinelli as her proxy. Any suggestion of his on the matter would be most welcome and reassuring.

Your Most Reverend Excellency,

1. Hoping to see the Rule finished any day, I delayed informing Your Most Reverend Excellency that the priest in Genoa of whom I spoke when God granted me the good fortune of meeting You has again gone to the Courts,1 and I cannot leave Ferrara, being occupied, as Your Excellency knows, with the Constitutions, in which observations and changes keep arising, now of words, now of other small things, which this Holy Cardinal thinks fit to remove or add.2

2. I sent my power of attorney to a Priest of the Cathedral, Don Accinelli, to deal with the matter.3 If Your Excellency has any means to suggest, or any instruction to give me on this, I shall be most grateful, and it will assure me that I am acting rightly, for these temporal affairs are so many afflictions to my soul.4

3. The Bishop of Acqui favoured me with a letter of commendation, undeserved by me, which I have already handed to His Eminence Cardinal Vannicelli.5

4. I dare not ask Your Excellency for a line for fear of being importunate; such was the comfort I had on receiving Your Most Reverend Excellency's most esteemed letter6 that I long to have more.

Deign to grant me Your Apostolic blessing, as with veneration I sign myself Your Most Reverend Excellency's most humble Sr. A. 8 ROSA GATT

She thanks him for the paintings of the Sacred Hearts and of Saint Anne. She is weighed down by afflictions but comforted by the thought that her life is being spent entirely for Jesus. In Ferrara much good is being done, both in educating girls and in nursing the sick, and likewise in Piacenza. May God's will always be done, and let us work; rest is for paradise, as the Saints now enjoy.1

A.M.F.

My good Father Agostino,

1. I have received a letter from the Superior in Piacenza telling me that Countess Caracciolo has sent her the Sacred Hearts and the Saint Anne. My good Father Agostino, I want to thank you in my own hand, though I am suffering immensely; I don't know where to draw breath; the weight of afflictions stifles me and saps my strength. My poor brain is in the mouth of Vesuvius; upheavals of every kind pour into it. Alas, I feel it can no longer hold me up!

2. One thing alone sustains me: God's will, as I believe I do in everything — to live for Him, to die for Him. The thought that these few bones are being consumed for Jesus is enough to calm all our agitation.2

3. So far there is nothing new about our matter;3 I am giving up the idea of coming to you because, with the heat increasing, I certainly would not manage the journey; so if they send it — and it seems there is still time — we will put everything in the hands of God the Father; He will handle His work, and I shall see my Father Agostino when he comes to Ferrara or elsewhere.

4. Those ladies who wanted to call the Daughters of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate, to Rome — are they no longer alive? What are they doing? Have they forgotten us?

5. How much good is being done here in Ferrara! 139 little girls taken out of the schools with the Jewish girls, and taught to love, know and revere the true God, the Church and his Vicar. What a consolation that is! We have admitted many of them to communion. What mercy of God! As for these foundlings, we are already beginning to take them into the house, rescuing them from sin. The nursing work grows every day: God be blessed!4

6. The boys at the Piacenza House number about 100, and great good is done there too; but [because of] the scarcity of providence, what suffering! That would be nothing, for it troubles me little, but the afflictions of every kind... My God, may your will always be done.5

7. What is happening in this city? Suffering, my Father Agostino seems to answer me. What is Father Bernardo doing?6 Ah! poor Saints, they are right; they suffered so much that, having reached that blessed abode, they rest happily and refresh themselves; I say they are right: "Enjoy it, for the blessed day will come for us too, and we shall do the same if we get there; only by God's mercy can we hope for it!".7 I alone am like this, because I am the most infamous creature in the world. If you see Father Angelini,8 greet him for me, and receive a thousand thanks together with all the greetings I know how and am able to send, as I remain your

poor Sr. ANNA MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

She replies briefly to her letter, glad of the good news. She should reassure the Superior in Genoa.1

A.M.F. My Vincenza,

1. Just one line to tell you I received your letter a few hours ago; I am very glad to hear so much news of everyone and of the happy meeting you had.2 I also hear what you tell me about Accinelli.3

2. Tell the Superior in Genoa that I received her letter and that she should not worry, there is nothing wrong with me; but you tell her why I am not writing.4 That is enough for now.

I am your affectionate M. R. for all ages, amen.

The Superior is ill again. She thinks eating fruit is harmful to her health. She awaits letters from her and urges her to take care. She should apologize to her mother. Instructions for the Superior: collect the Vernengo income and press Sr. A. Benvenuta's father-in-law to hand over what he owes.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I hear from Sr. A. Eletta of the Superior's poor health. My dear, the illness itself will have suggested the cause, but if she goes on eating fruit she will end up dying.1 It doesn't seem right to me, because the Lord does not command us to do anything against his will, and it is quite clear that by acting like that we go against his divine Will.

2. Today I await your letters anxiously, and tomorrow even more so. Since this morning I have had a bad headache pressing my temples — it must be the weather; I am much better as regards the breathlessness. How are you? Work, yes, but I order you to take care of yourself and to eat, but wholesome food, meat.

3. When you see your father and mother, apologize for the other time and say: "If I had obeyed it would not have turned out like this, because the mother had forbidden me to speak to you about it". To your mother, do you understand? You will see that you will be very glad of it.2

4. My dear daughter, I can't wait for you to come back; what habit does! I feel as if I had lost an arm! All this morning I kept saying: "I must write two things to Vincenza"; now I can't remember them; I think it must be the headache.3

5. Listen, tell the Superior of S. P. D'Arena that the income of the two Vernengo sisters goes to her, and that she should have someone write to Sr. A. Benvenuta's father-in-law to bring her soon the 800 F. still owed,4 because you know what the Paccani are like: se si lasciano chietare laco the moment never comes;5 she should press him by letter, and then use the money to pay for bread. Tell her that as soon as I can I will send her another cheese6 like the first; but if my head[ache] never goes and I obtain nothing, it is a sign they are not praying.7

Goodbye, for my head will have it so. I am your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

She is not entirely well. She approves what the Superior has done. She should give Carlotta's dress to Sr. A. Vincenza, who will go to Ferrara. Don Accinelli will not go to Piacenza, as Signora Airenta's son has died. Sisters will have to be sent to Genoa because an epidemic of typhoid has broken out

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I have just received your letter; I don't know what to think. The day Sr. A. Vincenza left the Superior wrote to you, and again yesterday; today I am writing in my own hand.1 The breathlessness continues; this morning it seemed a little better, but now it has come back, so I am suffering not a little; writing is painful for me.

2. Everything you have done is quite right. As for the girl with 800 F., you answered well: from this 15 F. a month and 50 on entry will be deducted; and for the postulant you told her rightly, 300 F. and her trousseau, otherwise no. That is the least that can be done.2

3. As for the pipes, wait a little; meanwhile have the rest done, because I expect them to come from Genoa.3

4. When Sr. A. Vincenza comes, give her Carlotta's little dress, the dark checked one with the silk bodice; she says she left it on her bed.

5. When Sr. A. Vincenza comes she will take Sr. A. Apanasia herself, and you are no longer to send Sr. A. Giovannina.4

6. Don Accinelli will no longer come this week, because today I had a letter from the Superior of S. P. D'Arena [saying] that Paoletta Airenta's son, Girolamo, whom you know, shot himself under the chin with a pistol and is dead. Imagine what grief the mere thought of his death caused me! Alas, my God, the poor old woman is in constant convulsions and will surely end by dying of it.5

7. There is a typhoid epidemic at S. P. D'Arena and Sisters will have to be sent there. I hope you received the letter in which the Superior told you about the Massari girl and all those going to the baths.6 Goodbye; I am your

Affectionate M. ROSA. Punish the girls if need be; keep Sr. A. Angelica under an iron hand.7

She constantly commends her to the Father, that he may assist her in her work. She hears that Accinelli is very busy because of the misfortune in the Airenta family. She should ask the Lawyers whether, if the case is lost, it would be good for the Vernengo sisters to take a mortgage on the Piacenza house. A visit by her to the Countess would be advisable.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I have received your letters: yesterday one from Piacenza, today the other from Genoa announcing your good journey. God be blessed for ever! This good Father alone knows how often I ask a blessing for my Vincenza and what prayers I said this morning that she might speak well to the judges, and that God might give us strength to suffer according to his will, and that she might obtain everything.1

2. I am making a novena to dear Our Lady of Graces. Dear Jesus, I am anxious until I have a letter from you telling me something about this.

3. I hear that Accinelli is very busy with the Airenta family because of their misfortune; you cannot imagine how painful it was for me when I read of it in a letter from the Superior of S. P. D'Arena.2 Patience; every day God gives us occasion to keep watch over ourselves.

4. If you can, I would like you to see whether you can get the pipes for the Piacenza water supply. You understand me, don't you?3 Ask the Lawyers carefully whether, if we lose the suit that might be brought against me, it would be good for the Vernengo sisters to take a mortgage on the Piacenza house. It would certainly be much better for me; try to get it done.4

5. My suffering has eased a little, I am a little better; don't worry, I am well looked after and cared for; of course it is not my Sr. A. Vincenza, in whom I have so much confidence, but I hope she will come soon.

6. I wrote to Sr. A. Apanasia to come; she will be in Piacenza and you will come together.5 It would be good for you to visit the Countess — I have already written to her — so you had better buy her a small box of sweets and take it to her.6

7. Goodbye for now; tomorrow I will write again; every day at 3 in the afternoon I sit down to write to you. God bless you a thousand thousand times and at every moment, as this poor mother of yours desires, who desires nothing but to see you holy. For pity's sake, beware of vainglory! Keep humble if you want God to help you.7 Goodbye; I am your

Affectionate M. ROSA

She should ask her uncle to agree to plead the case and tell the other lawyer that, since we are poor, her uncle will handle it free of charge. She has written and will write again to the Superior. She should look into finding a more suitable house for the Sisters.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. It is 10 \ and I have not yet received your letter; I am waiting for it. Here it is now. I have read it; you have done everything well.1

2. Listen, use the excuse that we shall not be paying your uncle, so that he can perfectly well take the case and the other man won't take offence.2 I am writing to the father asking him, for charity's sake, not to write to anyone.3 You no longer need to go to Nizza, but come as soon as you are ready; but for charity's sake leave everything in order first.

3. Arrange for your uncle to agree to take the case; go yourself to Bernardi and tell him that, being poor, we would like your uncle to handle it, as it will cost us nothing.4

4. I am praying, and at every moment, as I wrote to you.5 This is the third letter; tell me whether you have received them, because I wouldn't want them lost.

5. Tell the Superior I received her letter and enclose a little note for her.

6. The breathlessness oppresses me; but now and then there are moments when I breathe fairly well. Don't worry, it will pass. Today I shall hear on what day they will let me go free.

7. Listen, your letter arrived open, because you must have had it open and then not sealed it again.

8. Trust no one but your uncle; to all the others always say: "What can that priest possibly get, when we have nothing and live on Providence?".6

9. I hear about the Superior, but I am extremely displeased, because she brought it on herself by eating fruit.7 Enough; I am writing to her now.

10. Listen, my dear, see about the house, whether they could find a better one, more suitable for religious.8 I am receiving letters from Nizza; I hear Sr. A. Teresa is dying.9 I will stop for now; I am your

Affectionate M. ROSA

11. In complete secrecy, observe in detail the outward conduct of Sr. A. Santina10 and then write to me.

I am yours eternally, affectionate MOTHER

She has received her letters with the various news. She should get Don Accinelli to conclude the Vernengo Sisters' business and have them go to Piacenza. She feels the weight of the heavy debt. She asks for news of acquaintances. She should advise the Superior about the school.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I have received your third letter,1 and with this one I am writing it is the fourth, yet you mention only one; so be careful they don't get lost.

2. I hear of D. L.'s indolence.2 My daughter, don't you know that those for whom it is not their own cause cannot feel things as keenly as we do?

3. How painful it was to hear about Gerolamo. Poor mother!3

4. I wrote to Gigino that you will let him know when you return, so that he can tell you everything he wants.

5. Try to get Don Accinelli to arrange everything for the Vernengo sisters and invite them to come and take a mortgage on the Piacenza property.4

6. How those 2000 F. weigh on my back! Patience; everyone wants to console me, but everyone withdraws when it comes to making sacrifices — and besides, this is a holy promise, a strict duty! But, patience! My wickedness, my daughters, reduces you to this. I am very glad of the fine order there is at S. P. D'Arena. May God preserve it, because that is certainly what maintains good order; this news is the most consoling and gives me courage to bear everything.5

7. The Countess wrote to me; she wants me to go to Bologna, but my health is too poor; it does not allow me.

8. I was mistaken; I have received all 4 of your letters.

9. What has become of Maria? Is she still in Rome?6 Have you seen the Durazzo girl again?7 That widow who was to come — has the Superior seen her again?

10. She should see to the house; you could tell her what is new about her wanting to run a school. What a serious matter! I was right to tell her that this is how people get into a mess. If she has no use for the desks, she could give them to S. P. D'Arena; they are nice, and would serve for writing. You could hint at it, but don't let her know it comes from me — as if it were your own idea, if you think fit.8

11. I close so that this goes to the post by five.

12. I am a little better; indeed the breathlessness has eased greatly just now and I am breathing well; I still have a bit of a cold.

Goodbye; the Lord bless you, all the others and the Superior, and receive an embrace in the heart of Jesus, so that you may remain there to be sanctified.

I am your affectionate MOTHER

She is glad to write to give her a token of goodwill. She suggests buying a uniform dress for the little girls and providing for the Sisters too. She asks her to go to the Bishop to report on the house and to invite his Secretary to see the community and bless the chapel. Financial advice; spiritual exhortations.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter for ever

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. Blessed be God, this time I take pen in hand to write to my daughter to show her how pleased I am with her good conduct. Though my health and immense occupations give me not a minute's respite, I want to leave everything for a moment and pour out my heart writing to you, because our Eternal Father teaches me that tokens of goodwill must be given to those who deserve them, just as we must use the whip when there is need.1

2. The good news Sr. A. Vincenza writes me about that house — the silence, the order, the good little girls, the work — all show me that God is there.2 May his Spirit reign in your hearts. Work! Ah, where there is no laziness, there is surely peace.3

3. So, to give a present to these dear little creatures — though I have not obtained the grace — but I hope they will be encouraged to pray more and that I shall obtain it later — go to Genoa to the Jewish merchants who sell cotton cloth in the same building as Papa, and in my name buy two bolts of that cotton to make the same dress for all of them; it will serve them to wear when they go out to the seaside.4

4. Then I hear your Religious need habits; get them from the same merchant in my name; I won't tell you to economize on them, for I have ample proof of your economy.5

5. On 1 July the half-yearly payments of the two Vernengo sisters fall due, 500 F.,6 which will do for the miller; listen, when this month is a little further on you can tell him. Sr. A. Vincenza will have told you about Sr. A. Benvenuta's money; try to hurry it up; it is 800 F. and will be useful.7

6. It would be good for you to go to M. and report on the House; at the same time in the anteroom you will find his secretary, an excellent person; commend yourself to him and ask him to come and see you, bring his blessing to your community, and see the chapel.8

7. The cheese will come soon; if you need more nurses so that those you have don't overwork, write and I will send you two more.

8. Give my warm greetings to Don Luigi and the Vernengo sisters, to whom I will write as soon as I have a little time. Greet all the Religious; tell them that every morning, wretched as I am, I enclose them in the heart of Jesus; and the dear little girls too — let them pray that I may soon have what I so much desire.9

9. My daughter, these are times of tribulations and crosses; let us try to embrace everything with holy resignation; let us hold fast to the unshakeable tree of the cross, so that one day we may find ourselves saved and blessed for eternity.10

10. Let courage and resignation be our shields to sustain us in all the immense adversities met with in the Lord's work.11

11. It is very beautiful to know that we are nothing and that the work is for God and of God, the all-powerful sovereign, ruler of heaven and earth; He casts down and raises up in an instant, and we are all misery and confusion.12 Goodbye; I am your very poor Mother, who holds you in the most sweet heart of Jesus and is always with you, calling herself your affectionate Sr. ANNA MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

From her letter she has learned of the girls' deplorable behaviour and advises firm measures and sending home the one responsible for the disorder. She will send a trunk with various things. She should ask the master builder for an estimate for cleaning the house on the side of the large courtyard. She should press Grandi to send the masons to build the garden wall; then the pavement will be laid. Her health is somewhat better.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

1. I received your letter this morning and hear what you say about the girls, who are exceedingly naughty; I was horrified to hear about the novena; well, do this: call them all and tell them St Aloysius has heard them, and that those who made the novena should get ready, because I absolutely insist that they go home — and don't say it in my name, but in yours. One will be Giuditta Rusconi; send for her family without mercy and hand her over at once; so you will be rid of a hidden fox.1

2. An example must be given; you will see they will become good; and threaten Corina likewise. In short, I give you carte blanche: do as God inspires you.2

3. You will receive a trunk with the linen of Sr. A. Angelica,3 another with a small siphon, a box with two caps and two laces, one which Carlotta made for you in groscè and the other in tulle. Keep the tulle one carefully; for charity's sake, don't let it get dirty. The groscè one is for you, for the altar of St Francis, or rather of St Aloysius, a present from Carlotta. You will also find a lovely pair of very pretty slippers. Keep everything carefully for when I come. We will make the best use of it.

4. Now listen carefully. I would like you to ask the master builder how much it would cost to whitewash the whole outside of the house on the large courtyard, from the roof down, fill all the holes and then give it a reddish tint; if it were 100 F., well, it could be done at once. It really looks like a honeycomb, full of holes.4

5. I wouldn't want them to damage my plants; put the siphon wherever you think best, but in the courtyard, not at the sides, only in the middle; it seems to me it is needed there.

6. For charity's sake, go to Grandi and give him no peace until he has sent the masons to build the garden wall; then we will have the pavement laid; I think with a light scaffold they could do this job quickly.5

7. Today the breathlessness is easing, not entirely, but I feel much better; it was weakness. The pills have not yet arrived.6 Thank you; I hope I won't need them; the weakness was such that the slightest sciarato(?) they made upset me, as did the headache. For a few days I have been resting my legs, and so I feel better.

8. For Sr. A. Fortunata, try the Genoa pills, because I think she has something putrid in her stomach; try them, they can't do her any harm. The doctor has seen her; if there is nothing wrong with her lungs, it is a sign that her liver is upset; let us try.7

9. The Carnevali girl cannot be sent, because at S. P. D'Arena they are too hard pressed. See about sending even more to Acqui, which will do poor Emma's eyes so much good.8 Goodbye; I am your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

10. Today I ate and suffered less; I think

I shall recover this time too. I urge you to make an example by sending away the naughty ones. I would be glad if all the beds of the girls in the fine dormitory had white bedspreads.

11. You will find a parcel with a note for the Superior and things for the girls: two uniform dresses, one I had washed, one of Antonietta's and the other of Maddalena's; they wanted to make them for these girls, but we thought them ugly; for Piacenza they will be fine;9 anyway we shan't send this trunk until Monday or Tuesday.

12. When the Parish Priest comes, try to send him straight to S. Lazzaro.10 I asked the Parish Priest to come here and bring me his niece together with Panasia and her sister; and if he really comes, give Sr. A. Panasia that piece of white satin they sent you from S. P. D'Arena; if he doesn't come, give it to Sr. A. Vincenza, who will come [later] with Sr. A. Panasia.

13. Goodbye; send the Sisters' linen quickly,11 because they have nothing to change into. Show the other things to Sr. A. Angelica to see whether she has everything, and we will send whatever is missing.12 Goodbye.

She agrees to his plan: he may bring his postulants to Piacenza and his niece to Ferrara. She awaits him with her. He need not worry about the running of the Houses of Saint Anne. Any clarification of the remarks in his letter will be given in person.

Reverend Parish Priest,

1. I have just finished reading your letter1 and hasten to reply at once, so that Your Reverence need not delay carrying out your plan to take the two postulants to Piacenza2 and to bring me your most kind niece in Ferrara, whom I eagerly await;2 no less do I keenly desire to see Your Reverence and receive your blessing, and at the same time to have the good fortune of hearing Holy Mass celebrated by Your Reverence in our poor Chapel.

2. Your Reverence may rest assured about the arrangement of the poor Houses of Saint Anne;3 God the Father, in His Work, will know how to guide everything according to His Divine Will.3 We will discuss everything in person, including the reflections Your Reverence so charitably deigned to share with me.4

In haste, so that this may soon reach your reverend hands, I sign myself with all esteem and respect Your Reverence's most humble Sr.4 A.9 MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

I .

She is grateful for his little letter. She is much consoled by the news that in July he will be among the Daughters of Saint Anne. He will pass through Ferrara if she is still there. He will see the Sampierdarena House and its lovely little Chapel where one prays well. In Ferrara, on the other hand, there is wormwood, the bitter chalice of the garden; but it is sweet to her because it is Jesus' chalice and makes one strong.

A.M.F.

My good Father Agostino,

1. I have received your little letter and am most grateful for all you write about the Countess. Let us leave everything in the hands of God the Father; the work is his, He will see to it; I am capable only of spoiling things.1

2. Father Agostino, your news that you will be among us this July consoles me greatly. Who knows whether I shall be able to be in Piacenza; but if I am still here, you would certainly not go straight to Piacenza without first coming to us, poor Daughters of Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate.2

3. Today I shall write to Father Angelini,3 as I feel a little better; only the breathlessness still oppresses me, but let us hope it will pass with a little rest, as I have noticed that everything depends on my great weakness, and when I rest and don't move about so much I regain strength and the ailments cease, especially the shortness of breath.

4. The paintings are already at S. P. D'Arena4 and they are already praying for Father Agostino; I am sure that this time you will pay a little visit to that house and see the very good little girls, meet the director who guides them so well, and the many religious you don't know, and a Chapel which, in its small way, is poor but devout, and where one can recollect oneself very well.5

5. Father Agostino, there indeed one drinks good wine, but here in Ferrara it is the chalice of the garden;6 always wormwood; yet I find great pleasure in swallowing so bitter a drink, thinking that it is what my Jesus drank and that this is the chalice to which our Redeemer put his lips. What consolation, my Father Agostino, when I have the good fortune to put my lips to it; I would never take them away, but would stay sipping for an eternity.7 Believe me, it is bitterness that strengthens the stomach and makes us strong. Sweetness soon passes over the palate, but once in the stomach it causes nausea and brings softness.8

6. Courage, let us pray, and onward to the blessed day of our death.9

7. Beautiful month of the heart of Jesus! Let us hope that the poor Daughters of Saint Anne, M. of the Immaculate, may [receive] from this heart the graces they so much need, both temporal and spiritual.

8. I close because it is Sunday and I want to go to church for a while, where I leave you at the foot of the altar, remaining your very poor

Sr. ANNA M. ROSA GATTORNO

She is anxious for the news she cares about. She suggests bringing Sr. A. Eletta back with her, but then, on reflection, writes that she thinks it better to leave her in Genoa with the Superior.
